entries.content: The principal etiological and pathogenic factors are kidney deficiency; deficiency of blood, essence, and the Chong and Ren vessels; fading of the mingmen fire; qi and blood stagnation; and damp-phlegm blockage. Insufficiency of kidney essence and blood with weakness of the Chong and Ren, or waning mingmen fire leaving the uterus unwarmed (cold uterus), impairs conception, as does stagnation of qi and blood or damp-phlegm obstruction. Clinically the condition is accordingly differentiated into four types: kidney deficiency, blood deficiency, cold uterus, and stagnation of qi, blood or phlegm.

entries.content: Western medicine defines infertility as the inability of a couple to conceive after one year of unprotected intercourse; it affects about 1 in 5 couples in the USA. Etiologic factors are sperm disorders (about 35% of couples), ovulatory dysfunction (about 20%), tubal dysfunction (about 30%), abnormal cervical mucus (about 5%), and unidentified factors (about 10%), so diagnosis and treatment require thorough assessment of both partners. The financial burden and time commitment of diagnostic and therapeutic infertility procedures can cause marital strife, and failure to conceive often generates frustration, emotional stress, feelings of inadequacy, anger, guilt, and resentment; counseling and psychologic support are therefore important adjuncts to treatment.

entries.content: In Chinese medicine the main organ involved is the Kidney, and etiology is differentiated by the type of semen abnormality: oligospermia is mostly attributed to Kidney essence (Jing) deficiency, Kidney yang deficiency, Kidney yin deficiency, blood stagnation in the lower jiao, or damp-heat in the lower jiao; azoospermia to Kidney yang deficiency, Kidney yin deficiency, qi and blood stagnation, phlegm-damp, or qi and blood deficiency; poor sperm motility to Kidney yang deficiency, Kidney yin deficiency, qi and blood deficiency, or Liver-channel damp-heat (damp-heat in the lower jiao); poor liquefaction to Kidney yang deficiency, Kidney yin deficiency, or damp-heat; and abnormal sperm morphology to Spleen qi deficiency, Kidney and Spleen deficiency, Kidney yang deficiency with blood stagnation, or combined Kidney yin and yang deficiency. In Western medicine, causes fall into three categories: pre-testicular factors (e.g., obesity, drug use, alcohol, tobacco smoking, strenuous riding, medications, genetic abnormalities), testicular factors (e.g., age, Y-chromosome genetic defects and microdeletions, an abnormal chromosome set, Klinefelter syndrome, testicular cancer, radiation therapy to a testis), and post-testicular factors (e.g., infection, retrograde ejaculation, ejaculatory duct obstruction, hypospadias, impotence).

entries.content: Male infertility refers to the inability of a male to achieve a pregnancy in a fertile female after one year of unprotected intercourse. In Western medicine, factors related to male infertility are classified as pre-testicular, testicular, and post-testicular. Pre-testicular factors are conditions that impede adequate support of the testes, including obesity, drugs, alcohol, tobacco smoking, strenuous riding, medications, and genetic abnormalities such as Robertsonian translocation. Testicular factors are conditions in which the testes produce semen of low quantity and/or poor quality, including age, genetic defects on the Y chromosome, Y-chromosome microdeletions, an abnormal set of chromosomes, Klinefelter syndrome, testicular cancer, and radiation therapy to a testis, which decreases its function (infertility can be avoided by sparing both testes from radiation). Post-testicular factors decrease fertility through conditions that affect the male genital system after testicular sperm production, comprising defects of the genital tract as well as problems in ejaculation: infection, retrograde ejaculation, ejaculatory duct obstruction, hypospadias, and impotence.

As with Cloud TCM's exploration of other pains, for any painful location one need only first understand which meridians pass through that location to know both the cause and the method of management.

Viewed from the meridians, mother's thumb is very easy to understand, because the pain of this region lies near the Yangxi point (LI-5), on the course of the Large Intestine meridian and the Lung meridian. These two meridians are interior-exteriorly paired and, like brothers, are usually discussed together.

When the Qi and Blood of these two meridians are chronically abnormal (especially the Large Intestine meridian), the sinew channels (muscles) become diseased and muscular adhesions form; hence the symptoms center on the two tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

Whether in Chinese or Western medicine, easing these muscles with physical therapy or applying acupuncture can rapidly relieve or cure this pain.

Mother's thumb is intimately related to the Lung and Large Intestine meridians

But is mother's thumb really as simple as abnormality of just these two meridians? That may only be the result; deeper causes lie beneath. Two principal meridian phenomena can be distinguished here:

1. Deficiency patterns of the Lung and Large Intestine meridians

As noted above, mother's thumb is an outcome of abnormality of the Large Intestine and Lung meridians. When are these two meridians most prone to Qi-Blood insufficiency?

The answer is winter. In the Northern Hemisphere's early spring the weather remains very cold — sometimes colder than winter — so the probability is even higher then.

The colder the weather, the weaker the Qi and Blood of the Lung and Large Intestine meridians

Dr. Tseng Ching-hsiang, a rehabilitation specialist at Taiwan's Anderfu Rehabilitation Clinic, has observed that such patients increase by 20–30% in winter, and meridian data clearly corroborate this phenomenon.

By temperature, each day's lows fall at night and early morning; by season, winter and early spring are lowest — precisely the seasons when mother's thumb flourishes.

Doing the same housework, some mothers with normal Lung and Large Intestine meridian Qi and Blood do not develop mother's thumb, while others whose Qi and Blood are utterly depleted readily develop wrist pain.

What modern medicine has not specifically examined is that when the Lung and Large Intestine meridians are simultaneously deficient, besides wrist pain there are other pains (shoulder-neck pain, chest pain) accompanied by various symptoms.

Common ones include: fever, cough, wheezing, dizziness, chest oppression, nasal discharge, nasal allergy, diarrhea, itchy skin, and so on — all symptoms of meridian abnormality.

These symptoms are plainly those of the common cold. Thus after "external contraction of Wind-Cold," people whose colds were never properly resolved readily develop mother's thumb; a certain proportion of cases originate as sequelae of the common cold.

2. The Iron Triangle meridian pattern (Liver meridian Excess, Spleen and Bladder meridian Deficiency)

Modern medicine finds mother's thumb not hard to treat but hard to cure completely; the meridian perspective makes the underlying reason clear.

Virtually all refractory diseases are largely related to the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" that Cloud TCM often mentions, and mother's thumb is no exception.

Many people find it strange: is the Iron Triangle meridian pattern not in the legs? What has it to do with the hand? This must be explained through meridian correspondence theory, taking the most common variant of the Iron Triangle pattern as the example.

Viewed through meridian correspondence, based on the Zang-Fu Bie Tong (organ-pairing) correspondence, these two meridians correspond respectively to the Bladder meridian and the Liver meridian — verifiable by anyone who performs meridian assessments each summer.

Through virtually the entire summer, the Bladder meridian is deficient and the Liver meridian is in Excess; the chronic abnormality of these two meridians is also reflected onto the corresponding Lung and Large Intestine meridians.

The common meridian constitution of modern people, reflected entirely onto the Lung and Large Intestine meridians

Viewed through another meridian correspondence — the "same-name correspondence" — these two meridians correspond respectively to the Spleen and Stomach meridians, likewise verifiable by anyone assessing meridians each summer.

Through virtually the entire summer, the Spleen meridian is deficient and the Stomach meridian is in Excess; the chronic abnormality of these two meridians is also reflected onto the Lung and Large Intestine meridians.

The meridian chart above is in fact the most common meridian constitution of modern people — and it turns out to be the perfect meridian model for forging mother's thumb. Because constitution is difficult to change, a fundamental cure is very difficult.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern appearing en masse in modern people is, day by day, being reflected onto the Lung and Large Intestine meridians without their knowing it.

Once familiar with a meridian constitution, the pains that correspond to it can be clearly grasped

Therefore, anyone possessing this meridian constitution has a relatively high probability of developing mother's thumb when the hand muscles are used too frequently; and from the meridian perspective, even someone whose hands are seldom worked hard may still develop mother's thumb.

Cloud TCM member Mr. G shared in 2022 that during the nine-day Lunar New Year holiday he often stayed up late binge-watching shows, falling asleep at five in the morning for several days running.

On the afternoon of the seventh day of the holiday, feeling listless and wanting to brew coffee, he boiled water in a kettle and, on pouring, suddenly found his wrist extremely painful; checking the location, it was precisely so-called mother's thumb.

He immediately assessed his own meridians and confirmed it was indeed the Iron Triangle meridian pattern, then promptly massaged the relevant meridians; only after several days did the pain gradually ease. Once work resumed and he could no longer stay up nightly, his routine normalized and the pain disappeared.

In August 2023 a member shared that, for no known reason, pain suddenly appeared in the right wrist joint (mother's thumb); meridian assessment revealed no abnormality of the Large Intestine meridian, but an excessive left-right disparity of the Liver meridian — so this was very likely a pain phenomenon reflected from the Liver meridian.

Left-right disparity of Liver meridian energy, reflected as mother's-thumb pain in the right hand

Many pain phenomena in modern people appear on the surface to be caused by musculoskeletal lesions, since obvious inflammation and swelling are present. But from the meridian perspective, deeper causes can be discovered.

Most pain of unknown cause originates chiefly in each person's distinct "meridian constitution" — the basic meridian model that forges the various pains — and mother's thumb (chronic tendinitis) is one of its typical representatives.

If a patient with mother's thumb who presents the Iron Triangle meridian pattern continues daily under stress, accumulated fatigue, late nights, or disordered sleep, the wrist pain will be difficult to cure.

Of course, a single constitution can produce at least several dozen patterns, so there are many more possibilities; one may consult the content on Chinese-medicine pattern identification — expelling Cold, Dampness, or Heat pathogens from the body can all improve the pain of mother's thumb.

A Chinese-medicine practitioner familiar with every meridian constitution can, based on the meridians and their correspondences, predict the various possible pains and command the improvement of pain like the back of their hand, offering thoroughly complete solutions for prevention, treatment, and prognosis alike.

"Mother's thumb" is a chronic tendinitis with pain and swelling near the radial styloid at the proximal wrist, also tender on pressure; its modern medical name is "De Quervain disease" (De Quervain tenosynovitis).

Many mothers develop wrist pain after carrying a baby, wielding a kitchen knife while cooking, or moving household objects; the pain then extends into the index finger and thumb, until even holding a cup or phone or twisting a bottle cap produces stabbing pain. The incidence in women is more than five times that in men — hence the name "mother's thumb."

Some people, reaching for a toothbrush or wringing a towel on rising in the morning, suddenly find the fingers stiff and weak — the fingers will not close into a grip or they catch, the thumb feels powerless, and pain around the wrist steadily worsens. Mother's thumb readily appears in the early morning, which is termed "morning stiffness."

In fact, any work that constantly uses the wrist — daily vegetable farming, construction-site labor, even daily phone scrolling — readily produces mother's thumb.

Modern people constantly scroll their phones with the thumb, producing mother's thumb.

Modern medicine considers this condition difficult to cure fully and prone to recurrence once acquired, flaring especially readily when the temperature drops sharply. Some mistake it for "rheumatoid arthritis," but this pain improves again with slight movement.

Modern medical treatment of mother's thumb consists mainly of changing habits of use — not continually exerting the thumb; wearing a "brace" to offload the thumb's work; rehabilitation with thumb stretches and finger strength training; and physical modalities (heat, ultrasound, laser, TENS), among others.

No therapy of any kind achieves a full cure easily, and recurrence is common. This may be explored through theories modern medicine has not yet touched: the meridian theory of Chinese medicine is an excellent starting point and offers another option.

In antiquity, trigger finger belonged to the domain of traumatology; to Chinese medicine it is a disease of "sinew injury and overuse strain." To explore trigger finger from the meridian perspective, as with other pains, first examine the location of the trigger finger and ask which meridian runs along that route. On this basis, each finger has its own governing meridian, listed as follows:

Thumb: Lung meridian

Index finger: Large Intestine meridian

Middle finger: Pericardium meridian

Ring finger: Sanjiao meridian

Little finger: Small Intestine and Heart meridians

Trigger finger of each finger has its own corresponding meridian

When these meridians suffer chronic Qi-Blood insufficiency and the meridian sinew channels cannot be nourished by Qi and Blood, sinew-channel lesions arise and trigger finger appears; whichever meridian has the most severe Qi-Blood obstruction determines which finger is affected.

But could a person have every meridian in the body normal, with only a single abnormal meridian causing trigger finger? Absolutely impossible!

In most cases, one abnormal meridian is accompanied by a whole group of abnormal meridians — this is the meridian constitution. When one meridian constitution persists for several decades, one day a finger is found to have stopped moving: that is the genesis of trigger finger.

Accordingly, each meridian can be analyzed as follows:

1. Thumb and index finger: Lung and Large Intestine meridians

The thumb is the finger most prone to trigger finger, and large volumes of meridian data make the reason abundantly clear. The thumb lies on the course of the Lung meridian; since the Lung and Large Intestine meridians are interior-exteriorly paired, the Large Intestine meridian must be examined together with it.

The Lung and Large Intestine meridians are forever a mysterious pair: interior-exteriorly paired with matching energy trends. Strangest of all, their left-right energy disparity is excessive throughout the entire year, the Lung meridian most severely.

The Lung and Large Intestine meridians show excessive left-right energy disparity in all four seasons

In the interpretive techniques of Ryodoraku meridian assessment, an "excessive left-right value disparity" in a single meridian signifies "pain." So it stands entirely to reason that the thumb is the most pain-prone finger.

One member's son, only 25, typed phone messages with his thumbs for over five hours daily; within a few months he developed "thumb pain" — a form of trigger finger that can appear at any age. The remedy is equally simple: stop operating the phone with the thumb.

The index finger is likewise closely bound to the Lung and Large Intestine meridians. If a person constantly uses the index finger (e.g., one-finger typing, playing mobile games with the index finger) while the Qi and Blood of the Lung and Large Intestine meridians are chronically abnormal, trigger finger of the index finger readily develops.

2. Ring finger: Sanjiao meridian

Cloud TCM has noted in other articles (click to read) that the energy of the Sanjiao meridian moves almost in lockstep with the Lung and Large Intestine meridians. This is why the ring finger also readily develops trigger finger: these three meridians, as if by appointment, present Excess or Deficiency patterns together.

High interconnection among the Lung, Large Intestine, and Sanjiao meridians

The chart clearly shows that in March–April each year the energy of these three meridians is especially low. Sure enough, in March 2022 a member reported waking one morning from "index finger pain"; he said the stabbing pain was truly unforgettable — the first such symptom of his life.

After rising, he found the index finger hard to move. He later soaked it in hot water and kept exercising the finger and patting the Large Intestine meridian, after which it clearly improved. He said: "When I patted the whole Large Intestine meridian that day, it really hurt!"

3. Middle finger: Pericardium meridian

The middle finger is, after the thumb, the finger most prone to trigger finger — fully borne out by large volumes of meridian data, because a certain proportion of people have chronic Pericardium meridian Deficiency, and in winter the left-right disparity becomes very severe.

The Heart and Pericardium meridians show excessive left-right energy disparity from September through April

The issues of the Pericardium meridian are discussed in detail under "carpal tunnel syndrome" — which is why people with middle-finger trigger finger usually also develop "carpal tunnel syndrome" (click to read).[@ad:1]

4. Little finger: Small Intestine and Heart meridians

From the meridian perspective, the little finger should be the finger least prone to trigger finger, because the Heart and Small Intestine meridians are in Excess patterns almost year-round — meridians of robust energy whose Qi and Blood do not easily become obstructed. So if a person frequently shows Small Intestine meridian Deficiency, that is a signal demanding attention, and little-finger trigger finger becomes possible.

Moreover, the energies of the Pericardium and Heart meridians are interlinked; when both are chronically deficient, little-finger trigger finger also becomes possible.

The energies of the Pericardium and Heart meridians are usually interlinked

5. Common meridian constitution patterns in trigger finger

As noted above, no one's meridian presentation consists of an abnormal Lung meridian with everything else normal. Meridian abnormalities always appear as a group; such a group is a "meridian pattern," and a frequently recurring meridian pattern is a "meridian constitution." When a meridian constitution persists for decades, the associated symptoms or diseases appear.

Take the Lung, Large Intestine, and Sanjiao meridians: they frequently figure in the "Cold-type constitution," which looks like the figure below. If this meridian pattern is maintained 6–10 months a year for 20 years, it would be hard indeed not to develop trigger finger. And if in winter the hands are also plunged into icy water, triggering it becomes easier still.

The Cold-type constitution frequently shows Deficiency of the Lung, Sanjiao, and Large Intestine meridians

Take the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern": one of its variants involves chronic Deficiency of the Heart and Pericardium meridians, which readily produces trigger finger of the middle and little fingers, the middle finger being most common.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern can produce middle-finger trigger finger

A Cloud TCM member one day performed a meridian assessment for a friend with middle-finger trigger finger, and precisely this meridian pattern appeared. Once such a pattern has appeared, dozens of subsequent assessments will show similar patterns — a rigid, unchanging constitutional type extremely difficult to alter.

In the two charts above, the leg meridians are all severely abnormal. Could one treat trigger finger by attending only to the hands and ignoring the legs? Impossible!

Some skilled Chinese medicine practitioners can even treat trigger finger of the hand from the legs — and this is no fantasy. Dr. Huang Hsien-ming has shared his finding that the injury of trigger finger often originates in the feet, pelvis, and lumbar misalignment; the pelvis and lumbar spine are the "foundation" of the arm's fascia — when the foundation is unstable, the arm's fascia is not positioned correctly, and so it jams.

Since trigger finger is a phenomenon produced by obstructed meridian Qi and Blood causing muscular and fascial imbalance, one may directly release muscular adhesions in the forearm, upper arm, shoulder, upper back, lower back, buttocks, and so on, for rapid improvement.

Take Teacher Cheng of Taiwan, who has long shared methods for improving trigger finger through Facebook and LINE groups: without touching the finger at all, merely finding tender points around the shoulder and upper arm and kneading them open, the trigger finger improves by more than half on the spot.

Whenever trigger finger appears, resting the affected finger while changing the meridian constitution — patting the relevant meridians, with massage, gua sha, cupping, and so on to remove muscular and fascial adhesions — can bring clear improvement within a short time.

"Trigger finger," also called "snapping finger," is formally named "stenosing tenosynovitis of the finger flexor tendons." It most often presents as finger stiffness in the morning: after bending, the finger cannot straighten, and the other hand may even be needed to pry it open.

A sound or clicking sensation occurs when the finger is straightened, with tenderness or a lump (nodule) in the palm at the base of the finger; in more severe cases the patient may even be woken by pain in the middle of the night.

The causes of trigger finger are numerous. It appears most often in people with chronic overuse of the fingers, in whom excessive friction between the flexor tendons and their pulleys produces inflammation, swelling, and narrowing; after the finger bends, the tendon catches and the finger cannot straighten again.

Some people must frequently handle cold water, which induces vasoconstriction of the muscles and vessels, aggravating the circulatory impairment of the fingers and thereby producing trigger finger.

It occurs most often in women aged 30–35, of whom 20–25% concurrently have mother's thumb (De Quervain tenosynovitis) or carpal tunnel syndrome. Other occupations — massage therapists, teachers, chefs, dentists, machinists, assembly-line workers, homemakers, heavy computer and phone users, and so on — are all at risk of trigger finger.

Trigger finger is also often a symptom of other diseases, for example: tumors, infection, inflammatory disease, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, diabetes, or metabolic disorders.

Sometimes no cause for trigger finger can be found: inexplicably, one morning on waking, a finger simply will not straighten.

Any finger can develop trigger finger. Which finger is most often affected? Opinions differ, but the thumb is most common; the index, middle, and ring fingers are also possible, while the little finger is relatively rare.

When trigger finger appears, it is considerably troubling.

Treatment of trigger finger consists of changing living and working patterns to reduce overuse of the fingers, and oral or injected corticosteroids or anti-inflammatory analgesics to ease the pain of inflammation and swelling.

Physical therapy may also be used, for example: ultrasound, laser therapy, electrotherapy, finger splints, joint mobilization, deep tendon massage, heat application, paraffin baths, and so on. More severe cases undergo surgical release of the inflamed tendon sheath.

Why is the thumb most prone to trigger finger? Watch people typing with thumbs and index fingers on the metro or bus and the reason becomes obvious. As for those whose trigger finger has no identifiable cause, the meridian theory of Chinese medicine is the most suitable framework for understanding it, offering a new line of approach.

As with other pains, to discuss pain in a region, the most direct approach in Chinese-medicine theory is to consider which meridians pass through the lateral and anterior knee — usually it is abnormality of these meridians that produces the pain and the muscular lesions.

The anterior, lateral, and posterior knee are influenced by the Stomach, Gallbladder, and Bladder meridians

This article discusses the lateral and anterior knee, hence chiefly the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians. As noted above, modern medicine holds that women's naturally wider pelvis predisposes to friction over the lateral femoral condyle, producing iliotibial band syndrome.

The muscle groups affecting anterior, lateral, and posterior knee pain

Imagine someone whose Gallbladder and Stomach meridian Deficiency begins at age 10, who goes through life never knowing what meridians are and never maintaining them: by age 60 they have accumulated 50 years of Qi-Blood obstruction and muscular lesions — would the knees not develop problems?

Generally, people over 60 readily present the "Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency" meridian pattern, signifying insufficiency of Qi and Blood in all meridians leading to the legs, hence a greater likelihood of anterior, lateral, and posterior knee pain. Medial pain, of course, is no exception.

Obstruction of the leg's three Yang meridians produces anterior, lateral, and posterior knee pain

According to long-term observation by many Cloud TCM members, in most people with the "Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency" meridian pattern, knee pain manifests chiefly on the medial and anterior aspects, and sometimes the entire knee aches.

Viewed by season, entering winter readily produces "lateral" and "anterior" knee pain. Summer differs: summer most readily produces Bladder meridian Deficiency, so in summer it is instead the "posterior" knee that readily becomes tight or painful.

Winter and summer meridian patterns differ, so the knee regions prone to pain differ as well

If a person's meridian constitution features chronic Deficiency of the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Bladder meridians, then with the meridian Qi and Blood of the anterior, lateral, and posterior knee chronically obstructed, the muscles cannot receive nourishing Qi and Blood; the related sinew channels and muscles begin to form adhesions, bone spurs begin to form as organic lesions arise, and inflammation gradually develops in the patellar tendon, quadriceps, lateral collateral ligament, and popliteal fossa — anterior, lateral, and posterior knee pain thus appears naturally.[@ad:1]

Some people undergo acupuncture, tuina, massage and patting, cupping, even myofascial therapy or daily stretching, yet still cannot fundamentally cure their anterior, lateral, or posterior knee pain — entirely possible!

This is because those who begin thinking about health cultivation are usually already over 40; their meridian pattern has persisted unchanged for at least 30–50 years, becoming a "stubborn Yang-Deficient constitution." Muscles held tense and unable to release for decades will contract back again no matter how they are massaged or stretched.

An internally Yang-Deficient meridian pattern producing knee and elbow pain

Being fond of experimentation, the member asked him to test the effect of Si Ni Tang (Frigid Extremities Decoction), the most powerfully Yang-warming formula. Astonishingly, within half an hour of taking Si Ni Tang, the friend's elbow and lateral knee pain both disappeared. He said: "I have truly witnessed the power of warming-Yang Fire-Spirit medicine — modern people really are heavily laden with Cold!"

Case 2: This is a case observed for more than 10 years. Several years ago he began to have frequent knee pain; hospital examination diagnosed "degenerative arthritis." His knee pain was usually medial and anterior, and in cold weather the whole knee hurt.

At first he saw Western physicians and took "analgesics" and "non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs," which helped but could not effect a cure. Friends told him intra-articular injection of hyaluronic acid could improve this degenerative arthritis, but the need for repeated injections at intervals made him hesitant.

He later took glucosamine and chondroitin, both with noticeable effect, but the pain returned whenever he stopped for a while.

A knee-pain meridian phenomenon observed over more than ten years

He then discovered that whenever the pain flared, half an hour of far-infrared lamp irradiation would relieve the greater part of it, so he confirmed that heat therapy worked well for him. Later he regularly soaked his feet in hot water and massaged the relevant acupoints (Yanglingquan GB-34, Yinlingquan SP-9, Zusanli ST-36, Sanyinjiao SP-6, Xuehai SP-10), improving further. At times he found that massaging the Pericardium meridian could also, surprisingly, improve his knee pain, and from time to time he asked friends to knead his buttocks, which also eased the knee pain.

Since his Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency meridian phenomenon never changed, his condition waxed and waned; over more than ten years he grew accustomed to coexisting with his meridian constitution. Whenever the weather turned hot or cold, his knees would automatically notify him to commence his health-cultivation routine, which he undertook with pleasure; eventually he had a fixed SOP (standard operating procedure) for managing it.

This member said: "A few years ago a friend gave him a Mi Band, and to this day he still requires himself to walk ten thousand steps a day! Apparently knee pain no longer troubles him much."

Modern medicine habitually understands knee pain through bones and tendons. Understanding knee pain through the meridians, the cause of pain on any aspect of the knee can be clearly grasped; by easing the sinew channels (muscles) and improving the body's Zang-Fu, Cold-Heat balance, and Dampness, the majority of refractory knee pain phenomena can be greatly improved.

Knee pain is a common and complex pain. It is chiefly divided into anterior, lateral, medial, and posterior; what is discussed here is pain of the "lateral" and "anterior" knee. Modern medicine's understanding of knee pain is already extremely thorough.

Lateral knee pain is a relatively less common location of knee pain; modern medicine attributes it mainly to injury of the lateral ligaments, arthritis, and meniscal damage. Eighty percent of lateral knee pain is caused by "iliotibial band syndrome" (ITBS), with the pain point mainly at the lateral femoral condyle.

The high-risk groups for iliotibial band syndrome are chiefly women, long-distance runners, and cyclists; it is an inflammatory reaction produced by repeated friction of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral condyle. When the gluteus medius and gluteus maximus are weak or the hip is unstable, iliotibial band tension increases and lateral knee pain results.

Frequent runners are prone to lateral knee pain.

Lateral knee pain may also arise from ankle problems, incorrect running-shoe choice, poor running form, excessive uphill and downhill work, and so on.

Anterior knee pain accompanied by swelling and inflammation is very likely "prepatellar bursitis" or "patellar tendinitis (jumper's knee)," which frequently occurs in those who practice repeated jumping — basketball, volleyball, skiing — with pain from inflammation of the tendon connecting the patella to the tibia.

Pain at the upper margin of the knee may be "quadriceps tendinitis": the muscle arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine and the femur, gradually forming a tendon distally that envelops the patella. In some young people, the pain occurs at the "tibial tuberosity," the attachment point of the patellar ligament, with a tender point on pressure.

Causes of pain at the upper margin and front of the knee

Inflammatory joint diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, gout, septic arthritis, etc.) can also produce anterior knee pain, with the entire knee feeling swollen and inflamed, affecting knee flexion.

Modern medical treatment of knee pain, besides anti-inflammatory analgesics, may include injection of corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid, and similar agents, with surgery when severe, together with nutritional supplements (glucosamine).

Combined with rehabilitation, physical modalities (prolotherapy, shockwave therapy, phototherapy and thermotherapy), lifestyle modification, weight reduction, and so on; Pilates exercise therapy has also become popular recently, and yoga stretching is likewise effective — all methods familiar to everyone.

Modern medicine understands lateral and anterior knee pain chiefly from the standpoint of anatomy. If someone exercises little, has no injury, and the pain appears naturally with age or for no identifiable reason, then it is well suited to understanding through the meridian theory of Chinese medicine, which offers a new line of thought.

As with other pains, for lateral and anterior ankle pain one must explore which meridians pass through this location.

Understanding the ankle through the meridians reveals its complexity: do not underestimate this one small region — a full circle of the ankle contains all of the body's important meridians.

The lateral ankle chiefly carries the Gallbladder and Bladder meridians; the anterior aspect the Stomach and Liver meridians; the medial aspect the Kidney and Spleen meridians. So when a person sprains an ankle, these meridians and the sinew channels (muscles) they influence are injured.

Exploring lateral and anterior ankle pain through the meridians is thus inseparable from the Gallbladder, Bladder, Stomach, and Liver meridians.

The meridians to the lateral and anterior ankle are chiefly the Gallbladder, Bladder, Stomach, and Liver meridians

Ankle pain without a sprain — is that possible? From the meridian perspective, absolutely: the most common cause is simultaneous Deficiency patterns of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians.

The figure below clearly shows the two meridians are highly interlinked, and the colder the weather, the higher the probability of their appearing together.

The probability of simultaneous Gallbladder and Stomach meridian Deficiency rises as the weather grows colder

This is the chief reason why a certain proportion of people can spontaneously develop lateral and anterior ankle pain without any sprain.

Conversely, if these meridians remain chronically weak in Qi and Blood, with muscles, sinew channels, and tendons long deprived of Qi-Blood nourishment, then sprains occur at the slightest provocation.

A real case of anterior and medial ankle pain in February 2022

From 2022 onward, he developed ankle pain every year in the February–March period. The most recent episode was late March 2026: while working at his desk, his feet felt severely cold and his right ankle hurt intensely. Four consecutive years of this struck him as remarkable, and he actively reported it to Cloud TCM.

By then highly experienced, he knew clearly that warming both feet would resolve it, so he diligently warmed his feet, and two days later the ankle pain disappeared completely.

His case shows the key cause lies in Deficiency of the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Bladder meridians — Deficiency that actually begins on entering winter, while the true time of disease onset is chiefly in spring.

There may be two reasons:

The Cold accumulated through winter has persisted several months by spring, so the meridian obstruction is more severe.

As the weather warms and Cold seeks to leave the body, meridian energy rises, which also throws the sites of obstruction into relief.

Between winter 2024 and spring 2026 it was also found that in some members with the "Upper Deficiency, Lower Excess" meridian pattern, lateral ankle pain appeared, remarkably, when the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Bladder meridians showed Excess patterns. Below is one such case.

A man with lateral ankle pain presenting the Upper Deficiency, Lower Excess meridian pattern

In fact, this member reported not only lateral ankle pain but also chest oppression and chest pain, neck pain, upper back pain, stomach pain, gastrointestinal bloating, intercostal neuralgia, blurred vision, and so on.

His case shows clearly that whether the Gallbladder, Bladder, and Stomach meridians are in Excess or Deficiency, any meridian abnormality can produce lateral ankle pain.

Overall, pain is more probable with Deficiency patterns. Deficiency of all three leg Yang meridians (Gallbladder, Stomach, and Bladder) constitutes the so-called "Yang-Deficient" constitution: no problems arise in a warm environment, but stay in a cold, damp environment and troubles multiply.

Ankle pain is a common symptom. When ankle pain is mentioned, many people's first thought is an ankle sprain — rolling the ankle is especially common in basketball. Some people also sprain the ankle when they misstep in ordinary walking; nearly everyone has had this experience at some point in life.

With an ankle sprain, everyone sees a doctor, and both Chinese and Western medicine have very rich and detailed approaches to managing it.

Dr. Bao, a rehabilitation specialist, considers that ankle sprains can be approached from several directions: bone, ligament, tendon, nerve problems, and biomechanical problems (flat feet). Modern medicine's structural analysis of the ankle is already extremely thorough.

Ankle pain has several aspects; discussed here are the "lateral and anterior" ankle. Lateral ankle pain is usually caused by "ligament sprain" or "tendon strain," and 70–80% of sprains occur at the lateral ankle.

Basketball lovers know the experience best: full recovery takes 2–3 months. For "medial and posterior ankle pain," see the linked article.

Modern hospitals check for fracture, lateral ligament sprain, or posterior ankle ligament sprain, then grade the severity as mild, moderate, or severe strain and treat accordingly — this is highly professional.

Anterior ankle pain is pain of the so-called "tibiotalar joint," quite possibly "ankle joint effusion," "tibialis anterior tendinitis," or a "cuneiform bone spur." After a severe ankle sprain, the whole circumference of the ankle usually hurts (anterior, medial, posterior), and the likelihood of joint effusion rises.

When the tibialis anterior tendon is abnormal, its trigger points also refer pain to the anterior ankle. Bone spurs of the cuneiform (on the dorsum of the foot), which often form as bony overgrowth from friction, can also produce anterior ankle pain.

In this era, most people with ankle pain no longer go straight to a martial-arts (traditional bone-setting) hall; they dutifully go to hospital for a thorough X-ray examination and receive modern medical treatment.

For a mild sprain — or ankle pain appearing with no sprain at all — one may try understanding its cause at the level of the Chinese-medicine meridians. At home, using Chinese-medicine theory, improving ankle pain oneself can also be very rapid.

Many Cloud TCM articles note that symptoms which tend to appear only above a certain age are mostly the result of meridian obstruction accumulated over many years.

To explore plantar fasciitis, one must first understand which meridians chiefly pass through this region.

Of the pain locations mentioned above, the first lies on the course of the "Bladder meridian," the second on the course of the "Kidney meridian."

If the Kidney and Bladder meridians suffer years of Qi-Blood insufficiency, presenting Deficiency patterns, then over time sinew-channel lesions arise (degeneration of muscle, bone, fascia, and so on), readily producing pain of the medial sole, heel, and lateral foot, with rough, cracked skin at the heel (see figure below).

Sinew-channel lesions of the Bladder and Kidney meridians readily produce heel pain

Therefore, most people in fact have many years in which to prevent this disease. More than a decade before plantar fasciitis appears, the Kidney and Bladder meridians will already have shown several meridian patterns. According to the long-term observation of many Cloud TCM members, these can be classified into 4 main types:

1. A variant of the Iron Triangle meridian pattern

Within the Iron Triangle meridian combination there is a variant presenting "Spleen + Bladder + Kidney meridian Deficiency." In most people it begins appearing sporadically around age 20, usually transiently after staying up late or excessive fatigue, and more readily in summer.

After persisting 10–20 years, roughly between ages 30 and 40, intermittent medial foot pain or heel pain becomes possible.

With the Iron Triangle meridian pattern, foot pain appears once a certain age is reached

Since this meridian pattern is also accompanied by Liver and Spleen meridian abnormality, pain appears along those meridians' courses: pain of the big toe (gout), medial foot pain (arch ligaments), and lateral foot pain.

Cloud TCM member Mr. S once shared: "My situation is lateral foot pain, sometimes medial foot pain and big-toe pain — unstable. It appears for a few days after walking too much, then disappears naturally with rest."

Another member, Mr. A, shared: "When I was young it was fine; as I age I find the frequency rising, which makes me feel I have truly grown old!"

These pain locations lie plainly on this group of abnormal meridians, so they can be called the pains this meridian constitution tends to produce.

Staying up late is the surest way to produce this meridian pattern, so habitual late nights accelerate the formation of foot pain; the fastest way to render the Spleen, Kidney, and Bladder meridians deficient in Qi and Blood is to stay up late regularly.

If a person is chronically overtired, overuses the brain, and must constantly rush about, plantar fasciitis arises very naturally.

2. The Liver-Kidney depletion meridian pattern: Kidney + Liver meridians

According to the Differential Diagnosis of Symptoms in Chinese Medicine, the principal traditional pattern for foot pain is "Liver-Kidney depletion."

This derives from "the Liver stores Blood and governs the sinews" and "the Kidney stores Essence and governs the bones": when Liver and Kidney are depleted, the bone and marrow lose nourishment and pain results — a theory in which virtually all traditional Chinese medicine practitioners firmly believe.

Meridian assessment corroborates this phenomenon: in modern people the Liver meridian shows persistent Excess patterns from shortly after birth, and from the teens onward Kidney meridian Deficiency appears with increasing regularity. With advancing age, the Liver and Kidney meridians come to show Deficiency together.

The probability of Kidney meridian Deficiency in modern people is quite high — generally as much as 75%. When this pattern persists for 30 years, the various symptoms of "Liver-Kidney depletion" readily appear: dizziness, tinnitus, sore weak lower back and legs, fatigue, blurred vision, palpitations and insomnia, menstrual irregularity, scanty menstruation or amenorrhea, and other signs of aging.

Liver-Kidney disharmony is virtually the constitutional norm of modern people's meridians

In fact, chronic Liver meridian Excess with chronic Kidney meridian Deficiency pervades all kinds of meridian patterns. Tracing the root cause, plantar fasciitis arises chiefly from Kidney meridian Qi-Blood insufficiency.

Member Ms. Y once shared that over the past 10 years she has occasionally had morning heel pain; every meridian assessment without fail showed Kidney meridian Deficiency — years of identical findings proving this meridian phenomenon.[@ad:1]

3. The autumn-winter seasonal meridian combination: Kidney + Gallbladder + Stomach meridians

Modern medicine finds that plantar fasciitis occurs very readily in winter. From the meridian standpoint, simply observing the most common winter meridian pattern unlocks the reason.

"Kidney + Gallbladder + Stomach meridian Deficiency" is the most common autumn-winter meridian pattern, more pronounced the colder the weather.

The meridian chart clearly shows the relationship between Cold and heel pain

Many people show this meridian pattern from a young age; it appears most readily in winter and disappears in summer. In some people this winter pattern appears even in summer, indicating deep Yin-Cold within the body — this is the population at high probability of plantar fasciitis.

After winter set in at the end of 2021, a female member, Ms. C, began to have heel pain. She continued assessing her own meridians for over 2 months and found Kidney meridian Deficiency at almost every session, convincing her of how accurate the meridians truly are.

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that the common patterns of plantar fasciitis are "Cold-Damp congealing" and "Wind-Damp painful obstruction," which usually correspond to precisely this meridian pattern.

The Huangdi Neijing states: "Injury by Dampness is received first below" — meaning that people with internal Dampness readily develop diseases of the feet. Foot pain of this origin worsens in overcast, rainy, cold weather, with additional pain of the limb joints.

4. The Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency meridian combination: Qi-Blood insufficiency of the legs

Quite a few Cloud TCM members have gone straight to performing meridian assessments on plantar fasciitis patients and found that very many present the "Upper Excess, Lower Deficiency" meridian pattern.

This pattern is essentially the sum of the three patterns above, and skews toward women. Since it appears most readily in the middle-aged and elderly, foot diseases become more likely with age.

With the Qi and Blood of the lower body's meridians in decline, foot disease is hard to escape

This is understandable: when the Qi and Blood of a person's leg meridians are chronically lacking, the sinew channels and muscles naturally lack nourishment and begin to degenerate, so all manner of foot diseases naturally appear.

Hence not only plantar fasciitis: pain of the knees, calves, ankles, foot joints, and the various rheumatic joint pains can all appear in people of this meridian constitution — worthy of observation and study by more people in the future.

The fundamental reason plantar fasciitis is hard to treat is this: it is the result of meridian abnormality accumulated over decades. Unless the constitution is fundamentally changed, it will only recur again and again and is extremely difficult to cure at the root.

Based on the above, regularly patting and massaging these abnormal meridians and their acupoints, or stretching, can improve plantar fasciitis; soaking the feet in hot water or half-body baths also helps.

The Japanese physician Dr. Fumiko Ito has pointed out that with advancing age or cold weather, the Achilles tendon at the back of the heel gradually becomes dry, tight, and inelastic from poor blood circulation, forming plantar fasciitis and potentially causing knee pain, low back pain, and hip pain as well.

Half-body baths or hot foot soaks can improve plantar fasciitis

Using warming heat therapy to stimulate blood flow maintains the Achilles tendon, restores elasticity, and smooths its excursion. Soaking the feet in water at 38–40°C, or bathing the whole lower body from the buttocks down, effectively improves circulation in the feet.

Most important: after the bath, while circulation is good, massage and pat the three Yin meridians of the medial calf (Liver, Kidney, and Spleen meridians) — the effect is excellent.

One may also apply moxibustion, a hot hair dryer, or far-infrared irradiation to the heel and sole regions to improve the pain.

Modern women's fondness for high heels completely alters whole-body biomechanics, damaging the plantar fascia, knees, hips, and spine. Once plantar fasciitis appears, the days of high heels are just about over.

Shoes prone to producing heel pain

Some people find that flat shoes readily produce heel pain, because in flats the center of gravity shifts backward and the weight presses on the heel. Once medial foot pain or heel pain begins, stop walking barefoot or in flat sandals and slippers, and consider soft cushioned shoes or arch-support insoles.

Some Cloud TCM members have found that unsuitable shoes produce medial foot pain that resolves on its own after changing to another pair — evidence that ill-fitting shoes readily cause medial foot pain and even knee pain.

Heel pain (plantar fasciitis) is a common pain, characterized by stabbing heel pain the moment the foot touches the ground after rising in the morning. It eases after walking a while, but returns with excessive walking.

According to medical statistics, in Taiwan the number of people with plantar fasciitis, regardless of sex, begins climbing steadily from around age 30–40, with men accounting for 43% and women 57%.

According to the clinical observation of Dr. Hou Chung-pao, plantar fasciitis occurs most often at the heel (60% probability), next at the medial foot; these two sites cover nearly 90% of plantar fasciitis pain locations.

The two common locations of plantar fasciitis

Modern medicine generally holds that plantar fasciitis results from age or overwork: prolonged carrying of heavy loads, or gradual degeneration of the foot's muscles, ligaments, and tendons, increases the load on the plantar fascia and produces this pain.

Clinically, five groups are most prone to plantar fasciitis, in order: high arches, flat feet, excess body weight, habitual high-heel wearers, and those who habitually strike the ground with the heel.

Especially workers who must stand or walk for long periods — for example, market shoppers with heavy baskets and furniture movers — those who must carry heavy loads and walk frequently have a higher probability of this disease.

Modern treatment typically consists of anti-inflammatory analgesics or physical therapy (electrotherapy, thermotherapy, laser, or ultrasound), extracorporeal shockwave therapy, local corticosteroid injection, or prolotherapy.

Adequate rest, avoiding prolonged standing and heavy loads, reducing high-impact exercise and excessive walking, and icing during severe pain all help ease the pain.

Modern medicine considers the chief cause of plantar fasciitis to be "degeneration," so the older one is, the more likely it becomes; it also occurs more readily in winter.

Yet why do some people degenerate so easily while others do not? The meridian theory of Chinese medicine can offer a relatively complete explanation, giving patients a new line of thought.

Simply open the online 3D bronze figure and carefully observe the locations leading to the shoulders and neck, and six meridians can be clearly seen: the Bladder meridian, Gallbladder meridian, Triple Burner meridian, Large Intestine meridian, Small Intestine meridian, and Governing Vessel (Du Mai), along with vessels of the Eight Extraordinary Vessels (Yang Qiao Mai and Yang Wei Mai).

When the weather is too damp, since Dampness is a Yin pathogen, it also lowers the body's Yang-meridian energy, and neck and shoulder soreness appears.

Those with chronic neck and shoulder soreness who wish to cure it at the root must use Chinese herbal medicine or diet to eliminate Dampness and Cold from the body; only then can this pain be eliminated fundamentally.

From the perspective of meridian properties, the most fundamental way to improve neck and shoulder soreness is to eliminate Cold and Dampness from the body — this is what is meant by a root-level cure.

Neck and shoulder soreness appears most readily in Yin-Cold, damp environments.

Ancient Chinese medicine had no term such as 'temporomandibular joint pain,' but it did mention 'Kou Jin (clenched jaw),' referring to the symptom of tightly clenched jaws with a mouth that cannot open; similar terms are very numerous.

The four meridians involved in temporomandibular joint syndrome (Small Intestine, Triple Burner, Stomach, and Gallbladder meridians).

Temporomandibular joint syndrome readily appears in winter.

Over the past several years, members have continued to share how they improved 'temporomandibular joint syndrome,' and in particular they often worked from the 'Spleen meridian' and 'Kidney meridian' to improve this pain.

Taking 'Yuan-Luo (distal collateral) therapy' as an example, it frequently applies the correspondence principle of Zang-Fu Bie Tong (paired organ intercommunication): the Spleen meridian corresponds to the Small Intestine meridian. When temporomandibular disorder is treated starting from the Spleen meridian, the results are usually very pronounced.

The Spleen meridian and Small Intestine meridian share a Zang-Fu Bie Tong correspondence.

The 'Kidney meridian' corresponds via Zang-Fu Bie Tong to the 'Triple Burner meridian.' In cold weather, Kidney meridian Deficiency becomes pronounced and is naturally reflected in the Triple Burner meridian; and since the energy of the Triple Burner meridian moves in concert with the Large Intestine meridian, facial disease can also appear.

Methods for improving temporomandibular disorder

1. Heat therapy to raise the Qi-Blood status of the whole body

This disease readily appears in winter because the vitality index is low only in winter, which indicates that the circulation of Qi and Blood in the meridians of the whole body is very poor.

Therefore, if one can restore the Qi-Blood status to that of summer — exercising more in winter, whole-body meridian patting, frequently bathing in hot springs, whole-body far-infrared sauna, and so on — raising the whole body's Qi-Blood status helps improve the symptoms quickly.

Most TCM clinics use a heat lamp to irradiate patients; this is the 'far-infrared irradiation' therapy that substitutes for moxibustion. Frequently warming the muscles and acupoints of this facial region is a fast method of improvement.

In fact, one need not rigidly adhere to acupoints: simply massage the entire face, and even the head, find the more painful locations, pat or knead them frequently, and combine this with far-infrared irradiation — the results will be rapid and good![@ad:1]

3. Improve a Yang-Deficient constitution (Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency)

People of the 'Cold-type Yang-Deficient meridian constitution' readily develop temporomandibular disorder, because their Shaoyang meridians (Gallbladder and Triple Burner) and Yangming meridians (Stomach and Large Intestine) are chronically Deficient. The engineers of the Cloud TCM development team, who chronically overuse their brains, indeed have a rather higher probability of developing temporomandibular disorder — showing that this is already a predictable physical phenomenon, and this disease is entirely preventable.

Although temporomandibular disorder appears only in the head and face, it is a phenomenon reflecting the holistic influence of the meridians throughout the body. Therefore, without adjusting one's lifestyle habits and mood, simply hoping to cure this disease may not be an easy matter!

Headache is a symptom that has troubled the Chinese people for thousands of years, so Traditional Chinese Medicine has extremely rich experience in treating headache. TCM approaches headache from both its 'cause' and its 'location.' TCM holds that the causes of headache, as with other diseases, are divided into 'external contraction' and 'internal damage.'

TCM theory frequently mentions the concept of the so-called 'Six Pathogens,' which refers to 'Wind, Cold, Summerheat, Dampness, Dryness, and Fire' — six kinds of natural Qi, also called the 'six externally contracted excesses (Liu Yin).' This concept is of external origin, somewhat like what modern people commonly call catching a cold.

When the body is invaded by the externally contracted 'Six Pathogens' (Wind, Cold, Summerheat, Dampness, Dryness, Fire), the movement of Qi and Blood in the head becomes obstructed and headache appears; the most common headaches are mainly those caused by 'Wind-Cold,' 'Wind-Heat,' and 'Wind-Dampness.'

All of the external Six Pathogens can cause headache/migraine.

Because 'Wind' invading the body causes headache, and 'Cold' invading the body also causes headache, a headache caused by [Wind + Cold] is a 'Wind-Cold headache' — one headache pattern. Reasoning by analogy, many, many patterns arise, and every pattern has its corresponding Chinese herbal formula.

Headache from internal damage is mostly long-standing chronic pain, usually caused by internal damage to the Zang-Fu organs, Qi and Blood insufficient to nourish, and turbid Phlegm and static Blood obstructing the meridians. On this basis, the TCM patterns of headache are extremely numerous.

According to the current records of the Cloud TCM database, there are more than 1,400 Chinese herbal formulas that can treat headache — many people wanting to learn Chinese medicine would probably start getting a headache upon seeing this number?!

Only through database technology does one learn that the Chinese herbs able to treat headache are astonishingly numerous.

From the meridian perspective, the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) states: 'The head is the mansion of clear brightness.' The Qi and Blood of all Five Zang and Six Fu organs, the twelve meridians, and the Eight Extraordinary Vessels pour upward into the head; therefore the head is the meeting place of all the Yang, and also the meeting place of all the Yin!

After external pathogens invade the body, they cause abnormal movement of Qi and Blood in the meridians; whichever meridian is abnormal, the pain appears at a different location. Therefore, the ancients often diagnosed the cause of headache according to its location; the common classifications are as follows:

1. Taiyang headache

This type of headache mostly occurs at the back of the head, extending down to the neck and back. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Taiyang Bladder meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'tension (stress) headache,' and here it can also be identified as 'occipital headache.'

This type of headache accounts for the highest proportion and tends to occur in people with heavy work stress, emotional tension, or overwork, so its causes are related to emotions and stress. It usually strikes from afternoon into evening, and the greater the stress and the tenser the emotions (nervousness, anger, agitation, anxiety, depression, etc.), the more intense the headache becomes.

Meridian examination can completely prove this: anyone under heavy stress and fatigue has an extremely high probability of showing the so-called 'Iron Triangle meridian pattern,' in which Bladder meridian energy is extremely low, so occipital headache readily appears. Moreover, the Bladder meridian is active in the afternoon, so headache readily occurs in the afternoon.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern most readily produces headache.

More attentive observers will also notice that in this meridian pattern the Spleen meridian also shows Deficiency, which is why modern medicine also finds that this type of headache is accompanied by poor appetite.[@ad:1]

2. Jueyin headache

The so-called Jueyin headache is vertex headache, commonly at the crown of the head, and may extend to the eyes. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Jueyin Liver meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it also corresponds to 'tension (stress) headache.'

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern above can substantiate Jueyin headache: because of Liver meridian Excess, pain appears at the vertex. Cloud TCM member Mr. K once shared that his meridian pattern was of this type and he also had frequent headaches; he found that practicing relaxation and going to sleep a little earlier could improve this meridian pattern, and the headaches that came with it would disappear as well!

3. Yangming headache

This type of headache mostly occurs at the forehead and causes supraorbital ridge (brow bone) pain. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Yangming Stomach meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'cluster headache.' From large volumes of meridian data on modern people, the meridian pattern common in men very readily produces frontal headache and pain in the eye socket and supraorbital ridge.

The meridian pattern in which Yangming headache appears.

The meridian pattern common in women, meanwhile, very readily causes headaches along the pathways of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians.

The meridian pattern common in women readily causes frontal headache and migraine.

4. Shaoyang headache

This type of headache commonly appears on both sides of the head, the neck and shoulders, and the ear region. It is localized according to the pathway of the 'Foot Shaoyang Gallbladder meridian'; mapped onto modern medicine, it corresponds to 'migraine,' appearing most often in women — and the meridian phenomena in the figure above decode the reason behind it.

The Gallbladder meridian spreads over the entire side of the head.

A certain Cloud TCM member, Ms. S, observed the meridian phenomena causing her headaches over a period of as long as 8 years. She had chronic Gallbladder meridian Deficiency, the same whether in winter or summer, with the Stomach and Kidney meridians also frequently Deficient — this is the 'Yang Deficiency' meridian phenomenon often mentioned in Cloud TCM articles.

The meridian chart also reveals the phenomena of Wind-Cold headache and Kidney-Deficiency headache.

When winter arrived, she would very readily develop headache, runny nose, and sneezing — this is the 'Wind-Cold headache' caused by Cold Qi; and because Cold damages the Kidney, her Kidney meridian was frequently Deficient, so it could also be called a 'Kidney-Deficiency headache.'

Each time she encountered this phenomenon, she took 'Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang (Ephedra, Aconite, and Asarum Decoction),' which rapidly improved all her symptoms, and the headache quickly disappeared. For those who wish to understand in depth: if you study this herbal formula carefully, you will know it is a formula that dispels (Cold Damage) Wind-Cold and boosts Kidney energy and Yang Qi, so it perfectly matches this pattern.

Based on the four points above, the causes behind 'primary headache,' so intractable to modern medicine, are completely decoded by meridian theory. Since this article discusses simple headache, click 'Migraine,' 'Vertex headache,' or 'Occipital headache' for a deeper understanding.

In fact, treating headache is very complex — the acupoints that can improve headache are numerous enough to give one a headache. Just how many acupoints in the human body can treat headache? In the past, no one could fully clarify this, because the complete acupoint lists a human brain can memorize are actually few. Now, through the integration of computer software technology, in the Cloud TCM meridian-acupoint database alone there are as many as 140 or more regular-meridian acupoints that can treat headache.

Every meridian carries acupoints that can improve headache (migraine).

If these acupoints that can improve headache (migraine) are classified by meridian into a pie chart, one finds 30 on the Gallbladder meridian, 29 on the Bladder meridian, 19 on the Triple Burner meridian, 13 on the Governing Vessel, 11 on the Small Intestine meridian, 10 on the Large Intestine meridian, and so on.

The acupoint lists generated by data-analysis technology have completely decoded a millennium of acupoint indications and effects. Taking this headache article as an example, as long as you have performed meridian examinations over the long term, you can see acupoint recommendations that belong entirely to you.

Facing the most common headaches, patting the entire Bladder meridian (back, buttocks, backs of the knees, backs of the calves) and the Gallbladder meridian (outer thighs) can relieve the greater part. Alternatively, warming these two meridians with moxibustion, heat therapy, or far-infrared therapy can also improve ordinary primary headache.
