Diarrhea has undoubtedly been a common symptom troubling people throughout the past millennia, and the ancients therefore left behind many names and records describing it. The Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic), for example, mentions terms such as sun xie (undigested-food diarrhea), dong xie (cavernous diarrhea), tang xie (loose-stool diarrhea), shui xie (watery diarrhea), and ru xie (damp diarrhea), among others.

Diarrhea is primarily a disease of the stomach and intestines. These organs lie in the abdomen, through which a great many meridians pass. The principal meridians are the Conception Vessel (Ren Mai), Kidney meridian, Stomach meridian, Liver meridian, Spleen meridian, and Gallbladder meridian. The Large Intestine, Small Intestine, and Triple Burner (San Jiao) meridians also traverse the abdomen, and the Lung meridian ultimately connects downward to the large intestine; diarrhea is therefore closely related to all of these meridians.

Because these meridians show energy changes throughout the four seasons, meridian testing can be used to directly observe the meridian phenomena in people with diarrhea, revealing the relationship between the meridians and diarrhea. The meridian changes relating to diarrhea across the four seasons are summarized below.

1. Early spring: Deficiency of the Lung meridian and the three Hand Yang meridians

As the saying goes, "the whole year's plan begins in spring" — so let us begin with spring. For people in most regions of the Northern Hemisphere, spring is when nature's Yang Qi begins to rise, yet the weather remains very cold.

This sensation of cold can even feel colder than winter (click to read), and it does not change clearly and stably until early summer (May).

During this period, the meridian pattern with the greatest influence is the pattern of "Deficiency of the Lung, Triple Burner, and Large Intestine meridians."

As the figure below shows, this phenomenon becomes evident from late autumn (October) onward and continues until it peaks in late spring (April). This is the typical diarrhea caused by Deficiency-Cold of the Large Intestine meridian and the abdomen.

When the Lung, Triple Burner, and Large Intestine meridians are in Deficiency, diarrhea occurs readily.

According to the observations of many members, when a person contracts an external invasion of the six pathogenic factors (the common cold), since the Lung and Large Intestine meridians are an exterior-interior pair, abnormal bowel movements with diarrhea do indeed tend to appear.

Thus colds occurring between spring and summer also readily produce diarrhea — what modern people call "gastrointestinal flu" (stomach flu).

There is an even more severe version of this meridian pattern, in which the Small Intestine meridian of the three Hand Yang meridians also joins the ranks of Deficiency; in that case diarrhea is truly hard to avoid.

When the Small Intestine meridian of the three Hand Yang meridians also becomes Deficient, diarrhea is even more likely.

There are many causes of this meridian phenomenon. Besides the influence of external Cold in cold weather, Dampness is a "Yin pathogen" that readily damages Yang Qi; therefore, when using meridian testing to assess Dampness, one can also observe the energy of the three Hand Yang meridians.

Through long-term observation, some members have found that during rainy seasons, when the home is too damp, or after drinking too much iced water, these three Hand Yang meridians show Deficiency patterns.

Since all three of these meridians ultimately lead to the abdomen, diarrhea then occurs easily.

This meridian phenomenon is in fact what traditional Chinese medicine calls "Cold-Damp diarrhea": clear, thin stools without foul odor, abdominal pain, abdominal bloating, poor appetite, heavy limbs, fatigue, clear pale urine, a white greasy tongue coating, and a soggy or moderate pulse. This is diarrhea caused by Dampness encumbering the Spleen and Stomach.[@ad:1]

For most people, the energy of these three Yang meridians is quite strong and abundant. In some people who drink large amounts of iced water in summer, or whose abdomen catches cold during sleep at night, this meridian phenomenon also appears.

There are many such cases, and anyone can verify this at any time. Take member Mr. H as an example: he has used meridian testing for over 8 years. As a computer software engineer, he uses his brain all day long.

His Spleen meridian therefore frequently shows Deficiency. He observed a very particular phenomenon: whenever his three Hand Yang meridians showed Deficiency, he would begin to have diarrhea — most notably with the Small Intestine meridian — and after entering autumn and winter this phenomenon became very frequent.

Sometimes, when testing his meridians casually before any diarrhea had even started, the Small Intestine meridian Deficiency would appear, and sure enough, diarrhea would begin shortly afterward.

He was thus astonished to discover that meridian testing can truly predict disease — even foretelling impending diarrhea before it begins!

Deficiency of the three Hand Yang meridians readily causes shoulder and neck soreness as well as diarrhea.

One day, he saw TCM practitioner Dr. Yu Ya-wen's advice on television and tried eating Si Shen Tang (Four Spirits Decoction), red beans, coix seed (Job's tears), winter melon, and other Dampness-eliminating foods — and his diarrhea genuinely decreased dramatically.

As he gradually came to appreciate the importance of eliminating internal Dampness, he now places a dehumidifier wherever he regularly works, and his formerly frequent diarrhea has gradually disappeared.

Dr. Lu Zhizheng, chief state physician of Zhongnanhai, who has practiced medicine for over seventy years, noted in his book "Eliminate the Body's Dampness: Drive Away Spleen-Stomach Diseases, Skin Diseases, Chronic Diseases, and the Three Highs" that more than 90% of people have at some point fallen ill because of the Damp pathogen. In his lifetime of clinical experience, the "Damp pathogen" has become the greatest enemy threatening the health of modern people.

2. Summer: Excess of the three Hand Yang meridians

Continuing from the "Deficiency of the Lung, Triple Burner, and Large Intestine meridians" described above: upon entering summer, a dramatic change occurs — the three meridians that were originally in "Deficiency" transform into "Excess."

As the figure below shows, after May these three meridians turn to Excess, continuing until they peak in September.

When the three Hand Yang meridians show Excess, internal Fire-Heat combined with Dampness produces diarrhea.

Every reader can verify this phenomenon: as long as one does not drink too much iced water in summer, almost everyone's three Hand Yang meridians are in Excess — especially the Large Intestine and Triple Burner meridians.

At this stage, this readily combines with summer's dominant climatic factor (Dampness) to produce acute Damp-Heat diarrhea: yellow watery stools or stools with mucus, foul fishy odor, abdominal pain, burning pain of the anus, dry mouth and thirst, chest oppression, yellow urine, a yellow greasy tongue coating, and a slippery rapid pulse.

Cloud TCM articles often mention that Excess of the Triple Burner meridian can indicate internal Fire; the higher the internal Fire, the higher the Triple Burner meridian's energy, and many members have reported confirming this phenomenon themselves.

One member's situation was a severe year-round Triple Burner Excess, with energy frequently reaching above 150.

In many people with strong internal Fire, the three Hand Yang meridians all show Excess.

She found that each time she took Fire-draining Chinese herbs, her Triple Burner meridian would indeed come down. On one occasion she ate spicy hot pot (mala hot pot) and afterward developed diarrhea with very foul-smelling stools.

Consulting Chinese medical texts, she found this was very likely caused by excessive internal Heat, and after taking Gegen Qinlian Tang (Kudzu, Scutellaria and Coptis Decoction) she recovered rapidly.

One day, chatting with a TCM physician about this case, that physician also shared that whenever patients suffered hangover with diarrhea from drinking too much alcohol, he would prescribe Wei Ling Tang (Stomach-Calming Poria Decoction) with excellent results. This too is caused by alcohol generating excessive accumulated Heat in the body.

This change in meridian phenomena may well be the cause of what ancient China called "warm diseases" (wen bing): in winter, the Cold pathogen lies latent in the body, and only after Yang Qi gradually rises in spring does a series of cold-like symptoms of illness appear (latent Qi), reflected in Excess of these three meridians.

3. Summer: Liver meridian exuberant, Spleen meridian deficient (Wood overcontrolling Earth)

TCM often says "nourish the Liver in spring, nourish the Heart in summer," and tradition holds that spring and summer are chiefly the seasons of "Liver disease" or "Heart disease."

In fact, observation of large volumes of meridian data from modern people shows that the most obvious change after entering summer is that Liver meridian energy becomes overly strong while Spleen meridian energy becomes very weak — something easily verified for oneself.

This fully confirms the Five Phases principle of Chinese medicine: once Liver meridian energy rises rapidly and Wood Qi becomes exuberant, the energy of the Spleen meridian, which belongs to Earth, duly begins to decline — operating by this same law every year.

For people living near the equator, where it is spring-like year round, if they do not spend long periods in air-conditioned rooms, their meridian pattern is virtually like this all year.

After entering spring and summer, most people show Liver meridian Excess with Spleen meridian Deficiency.

Diarrhea of this pattern corresponds, per the descriptions in authoritative TCM texts, to "Liver constraint overwhelming the Spleen" (Liver Qi invading the Spleen and Stomach) and "Spleen Deficiency with food stagnation" types of diarrhea; summer "Damp-Heat" also causes diarrhea.

Therefore, each year after April-May in the Northern Hemisphere, diarrhea becomes a common symptom, and the most commonly used formulas are Si Ni San (Frigid Extremities Powder) and Tong Xie Yao Fang (Essential Formula for Painful Diarrhea).

Million-copy bestselling author and TCM physician Dr. Wu Guozhong, in his book "Nourish Yang Qi: Raising Your Own Yang Qi Is the Remedy for All Diseases," also stated his view that the pathogen most invasive of modern people's Yang Qi is the Damp pathogen.

Most of the body's Dampness arises from Spleen Deficiency, because a poor transportation-transformation capacity of the Spleen leads to Dampness accumulating. Thus a person with Spleen Deficiency and heavy Dampness will very easily develop diarrhea.[@ad:1]

4. Early autumn: Spleen meridian Deficiency and Large Intestine Excess at their extreme

Continuing from the above, the Spleen meridian's Deficiency grows progressively worse from April onward, and it is upon truly entering early autumn — between the solar terms Beginning of Autumn (Liqiu) and End of Heat (Chushu), i.e., August-September each year — that the weather reaches its hottest extreme (the "autumn tiger" heat wave).

At this time the body's Large Intestine meridian energy reaches its most exuberant of the year, while the Spleen meridian reaches its lowest point of the year.

In early autumn, Spleen meridian Deficiency and Large Intestine meridian Excess both reach their extremes.

At this time, because the weather is sweltering and southern East Asia frequently receives heavy rains, so-called "Damp-Heat diarrhea" and "Spleen-Deficiency diarrhea" appear most readily.

In 2021, one member reported that after entering August, with frequent heavy rains, he often had diarrhea three times a day, with thirst, yellow urine, and very foul-smelling stools. His meridian chart showed Excess of the Large Intestine and Triple Burner meridians with severe Spleen meridian Deficiency.

The meridian phenomena of diarrhea beginning after entry into early autumn.

The cause of this diarrhea is in fact the same as in summer, only its severity is more pronounced. Modern medicine has found that after entering autumn, the probability of diarrhea caused by infections — chiefly rotavirus — rises.

Coincidentally, during this period the meridians also enter this diarrhea-prone stage. Perhaps it is because immunity is low at this time and resistance to viruses is weakened that disease has the opportunity to develop.

5. Winter: Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency, Yang Deficiency of the legs

Modern medicine observes that each year, from autumn onward — September to January of the following year, and especially October through December — is the peak period for epidemic diarrhea. Besides viruses, cold weather is also a cause of diarrhea.

Dr. Wang Hongyuan has pointed out that this is because cold weather triggers the gastrointestinal sympathetic nerves, prompting frequent gastrointestinal peristalsis and causing diarrhea; compared with the intestines, the stomach is more susceptible to climate. This is a modern anatomical interpretation of the TCM mechanism by which Cold causes diarrhea.

This too can be traced through observation of meridian phenomena: after entering winter there is a high probability of Deficiency of the Gallbladder, Stomach, Kidney, and Spleen meridians — this is what traditional Chinese medicine commonly calls "Kidney-Deficiency diarrhea" or "Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency" diarrhea. People with this diarrhea-prone constitution ordinarily tend to have abdominal pain, frequent bowel movements, poor appetite, indigestion, sore lower back, cold limbs, easy fatigue, and low spirits.

Member Mr. S was often forced out of bed by abdominal pain in the early morning. After November 2020, when Taiwan began to turn cold, he found that his meridian chart automatically became a Yang-Deficiency chart. At the time he searched Google, found the term "fifth-watch diarrhea" (daybreak diarrhea), and discovered it truly matched his symptoms.

As a planning specialist who overuses his brain, he shows Spleen meridian Deficiency in all four seasons; after winter arrived he found his Kidney meridian also showed Deficiency. He said: "At that moment, I truly saw with my own eyes what 'Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency' means."

Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency causing diarrhea can be seen clearly from the chart.

From his meridian chart one can also clearly see Deficiency of the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians (Yang meridians) — truly Yang Deficiency plus Spleen-Kidney Yang Deficiency in the fullest sense.

Having confirmed this pattern, and being fond of studying Chinese medicine, he bought a bottle of Si Shen Wan (Four Spirits Pill) in scientific (granule) form to take; its ingredients are nutmeg (Rou Dou Kou), psoralea (Bu Gu Zhi), schisandra (Wu Wei Zi), evodia (Wu Zhu Yu), fresh ginger, and jujube. After only a few days of taking it, his diarrhea genuinely improved by more than half — this is the main reason he loves studying Chinese medicine.

In March 2022 he gave an update: "To this day, I still often get diarrhea when the weather turns cold, and it still improves quickly after taking the medicine. But my meridian pattern remains the same — clearly, a Cold-type Yang-Deficient constitution is truly not easy to change!"

Fundamentals for improving chronic diarrhea

The meridian patterns causing diarrhea across the four seasons have been clearly laid out above, and they share consistent underlying causes. With attention to health cultivation, frequent diarrhea can be avoided, summarized as follows:

1. Eat fewer raw, cold, and cooling foods

As noted above, warming the abdomen can improve diarrhea; conversely, making the abdomen colder makes diarrhea worse. Therefore, if diarrhea appears during autumn and winter, one must reduce or stop eating raw, cold, and cooling foods.

The concept of eating fewer raw and cold foods dates back to the Han dynasty: the chief dietary prohibition when taking Gui Zhi Tang (Cinnamon Twig Decoction) for colds was to avoid raw and cold foods — a concept that has been followed for nearly two thousand years.

Eating fewer raw and cold foods can improve autumn-winter diarrhea.

If a person's Spleen and Stomach are already weak, and in summer the Spleen meridian is Deficient as well, and they then drink iced water and eat watermelon, causing Deficiency of the three Hand Yang meridians, it will be very hard to avoid diarrhea.

2. Dietary therapy or Chinese herbs to eliminate internal Dampness

Chinese medicine has many herbs and foods that expel internal Dampness; Cloud TCM has compiled a number of them over the past several years, and readers are advised to read and apply them (click to open).

Shen Ling Baizhu San (Ginseng, Poria and White Atractylodes Powder) must be mentioned here — its ingredients are nearly all foods. Member Ms. J once shared: "Shen Ling Baizhu San works like magic for me; there has hardly ever been a time it failed to stop my diarrhea!" Using dietary therapy to improve health is the concept people accept most readily.

In fact, judging from this formula's composition, it can hardly be called medicine at all — it is essentially a collection of foods, a dietary-therapy product worth promoting.

Its ingredients are: licorice (Gan Cao), fresh ginger, jujube, white hyacinth bean (Bai Bian Dou), white atractylodes (Bai Zhu), poria (Fu Ling), platycodon (Jie Geng), lotus seed (Lian Zi), ginseng (Ren Shen), amomum (Sha Ren), Chinese yam (Shan Yao), and coix seed (Yi Yi Ren). These ingredients can also be simmered into a medicinal congee.

The ingredients above are numerous; there is a simpler, scaled-down medicinal-diet version — Si Shen Tang (Four Spirits Soup), composed of poria, Chinese yam, lotus seed, euryale seed (Qian Shi), and coix seed. Many vendors add pork small intestine and stew them together; this too can improve diarrhea, promote digestion, and thereby adjust the constitution and strengthen resistance.

Ms. M had long felt Deficiency-Cold in her abdomen; whenever she ate watermelon she would invariably get diarrhea, and meridian testing indeed showed frequent Deficiency of her three Hand Yang meridians.

Diarrhea (loose bowels) is quite a common symptom, referring to overly frequent bowel movements and unformed stools that are liquid or loose; in severe cases there is dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, progressing to fever, shock, and even cardiac arrhythmia.

Modern medicine observes that the main causes of diarrhea are intestinal infection by epidemic viruses, bacteria, or parasites, or improperly stored food (moldy or contaminated with bacteria), causing 'gastroenteritis.'

Some people also develop diarrhea after consuming particular sensitizing foods (for example: milk, greasy or spicy foods, etc.).

Certain diseases present with diarrhea, for example: irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), endocrine disorders (hyperthyroidism), lactose intolerance, acute poisoning, dysentery, and so on.

Some medications or nutritional supplements have diarrhea as a side effect. Ordinarily, diarrhea resolves on its own. If a person has diarrhea accompanied simultaneously by fever, dizziness, chills, vomiting, or abdominal cramping, this is no longer simple diarrhea and requires examination at a hospital.

The modern medical community has observed that diarrhea often appears in the autumn and winter seasons, with October through December especially being the peak epidemic period. This is caused by a series of viruses led by 'rotavirus' and is also accompanied by some cold-like symptoms, for example: runny nose, fever, and vomiting — evidently diarrhea has seasonal characteristics.

In the autumn and winter seasons there are quite a few epidemic viruses that can cause diarrhea.

However, some people find that as soon as the weather turns cold or it rains, the abdomen begins to ache dully and diarrhea begins — this presumably does not belong to diarrhea caused by viral infection.

If viewed from the perspective of the TCM meridians, diarrhea may not have much to do with viruses, being instead a bodily response influenced by the weather; this common symptom can be observed from other angles.

The symptom of vomiting has troubled people in China for well over a millennium. Ancient medical classics such as the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) and the Shanghan Zabing Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases) almost all discuss it, accumulating a wealth of therapeutic experience and case records.

Vomiting and nausea often appear together: nausea may be a precursor to vomiting, and vomiting is usually accompanied by nausea, but nausea does not necessarily lead to vomiting. This article primarily addresses the expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth.

Because vomiting is a common clinical symptom, the Cloud TCM database has accumulated a large volume of meridian data recorded on the very day patients experienced vomiting.

If these meridian data can be combined with traditional TCM pattern (syndrome) analysis, this not only further corroborates the ancients' inferences about patterns, but can also advance modern TCM's understanding and application of the mechanisms of vomiting.

The ancients held that vomiting arises from the following patterns, described in turn below:

1. External invasion of Wind-Cold

The ancients believed that vomiting most readily arises during the common cold, and that summer "Summerheat-Damp colds" are even more likely to cause vomiting.

The ancients understood the common cold as chiefly two situations: one is "Cold pathogen invading the body surface," the other is "Summerheat-Damp" impairing the body's defensive function.

The Shanghan Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage) states: "Whether fever has appeared or not, there is invariably aversion to cold, body pain, and retching counterflow, with tight Yin and Yang pulses" — Wind-Cold colds can cause vomiting.

Cold damage from external invasion may present with nausea and vomiting.

This type of vomiting occurs because the Cold pathogen envelops the skin, preventing the body's Yang Qi from dispersing normally; unable to vent outward, the Qi accumulates internally, causing Stomach Qi to ascend counterflow and triggering vomiting. Gui Zhi Tang (Cinnamon Twig Decoction) is most often used to regulate this.

In the Summerheat-Damp type of cold affecting the body, vomiting occurs because Dampness encumbers the Middle Burner (i.e., gastrointestinal function is affected); besides vomiting, there are also epigastric and abdominal distension and oppression, poor appetite, heaviness of the body, weakness of the limbs, and similar symptoms. Huoxiang Zhengqi San (Agastache Qi-Correcting Powder) is most often used for regulation.

Since the common cold has no specific meridian pattern — the meridian pattern during a cold is usually whatever pattern the person commonly shows in daily life — the various possibilities discussed below may be consulted.[@ad:1]

2. Stomach Cold

The ancients held that Stomach Cold most readily produces vomiting. If a person's Spleen and Stomach are inherently weak (insufficient Middle Burner Yang Qi), they will easily regurgitate and vomit shortly after meals, often accompanied by stomach pain, belching, aversion to cold, emaciation, and weakness of the limbs.

The most common presentation is that suddenly eating too much raw, cold food provokes intense stomach pain; when vomiting, large amounts of clear fluid come up first, followed by the food just eaten, and the person feels more comfortable after vomiting.

Verifying vomiting caused by Stomach Cold is quite easy: many meridian presentations at the time of vomiting show the so-called Yang-Deficiency meridian phenomenon (see figure below).

The meridian pattern of vomiting from Stomach Cold.

For vomiting caused by Stomach Cold, the treatment principles are to warm the stomach, dispel Cold, and subdue the counterflow ascent of Stomach Qi; the commonly used formulas are Lizhong Tang (Center-Rectifying Decoction) and Fuzi Lizhong Tang (Aconite Center-Rectifying Decoction).

3. Stomach Heat

A phenomenon repeatedly confirmed by large volumes of meridian data from modern people is that the great majority of diseases are the result of extreme internal Cold or extreme internal Heat.

Thus, just as Stomach Cold causes vomiting, Stomach Heat also causes vomiting — and the probability of Stomach-Heat vomiting is indeed quite high.

Vomiting caused by Stomach Heat is usually accompanied by acid reflux, belching with a sour, rotten odor (putrid eructation), bad breath, a feeling of distension and oppression in the stomach, darker yellow urine, and constipation.

This situation mostly arises from an overly greasy or spicy diet, or habitual alcohol consumption, which causes Damp-Heat to accumulate in the Middle Burner (the stomach region); besides vomiting, there are Stomach-Heat symptoms such as acid regurgitation, halitosis, epigastric oppression, constipation, and a thick yellow tongue coating.

Among the many cases in the Cloud TCM database, it has been found that Excess of the Stomach and Gallbladder meridians, indicating strong internal Fire, is indeed readily associated with vomiting (see figure below).

The Stomach-Heat vomiting meridian pattern: Stomach meridian Excess with Pericardium meridian Deficiency.

The phenomenon most worth observing is that when the Stomach meridian is in Excess, the Pericardium meridian usually shows Deficiency. This corroborates the truth of the traditional TCM "zang-fu paired-communication (bie tong) theory," which is why the Pericardium meridian's Neiguan point (PC-6) has been used for a thousand years to treat nausea and vomiting.

The most commonly used method is to apply bitter, cold-natured Chinese herbs to drain Stomach Fire, and the effect is usually very rapid.

4. Liver-Stomach disharmony

Large volumes of meridian data from modern people show that many datasets combining Liver meridian and Stomach meridian abnormality are associated with vomiting.

This meridian pattern is usually accompanied by Deficiency of the Spleen and Bladder meridians, forming the typical "Iron Triangle" meridian pattern. Because real cases are so numerous, the meridian charts of 9 individuals are presented together below:

Common meridian patterns of vomiting from Liver-Stomach disharmony.

All of these real meridian findings were recorded during episodes of vomiting or nausea, clearly showing severe Excess of the Liver and Stomach meridians — a state highly prone to Liver-Stomach disharmony.

This situation is usually a long-term, chronic phenomenon: Liver Qi becomes constrained and does not flow smoothly, disturbing the stomach's normal function, causing Stomach Qi to ascend counterflow, with frequent vomiting and nausea that are nonetheless not so intense as to be unbearable. Besides vomiting, there are also chest oppression, epigastric fullness and distension, pain around the ribs, a bitter taste in the mouth, and so on.

During emotional fluctuations (such as anger, heavy stress, or anxiety), the vomiting worsens; Xiao Chaihu Tang (Minor Bupleurum Decoction) combined with Zuo Jin Wan (Left Metal Pill) is most often used to bring improvement.

Anyone can verify this personally: people who are frequently prone to anger or emotional depression do indeed readily develop the "Iron Triangle" meridian pattern, and thence various diseases of the digestive system.

In addition, traditional Chinese medicine holds that Stomach Yin Deficiency can also cause vomiting, which may be an extension of Liver-Stomach disharmony. Likewise, food damage (overeating) can cause vomiting, which is consistent with the understanding of modern medicine.

From the meridian patterns summarized above it is also clear that many symptoms share similar underlying meridian phenomena; how to improve these meridian phenomena is the key secret to preventing and treating disease.

If a person remains long-term in the meridian states described above, they will very easily vomit when they fall ill — something everyone can verify for themselves.

Vomiting is a common physiological response that can arise from many causes involving the digestive system, central nervous system, endocrine system, and other origins.

Digestive-system causes include gastroenteritis (caused by viral or bacterial infection), food poisoning, gastroesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer, intestinal obstruction, and so on.

Central nervous system causes include migraine, increased intracranial pressure (brain tumor, intracerebral hemorrhage), and motion sickness (carsickness, seasickness), which stimulate the vomiting center and induce vomiting.

Some pregnant women experience nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy (morning sickness); vomiting also occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis, and certain drug side effects and emotional stress can likewise cause vomiting.

The causes of vomiting are many and varied. Episodes of unexplained vomiting in daily life can also be explored from the perspective of TCM meridians, offering a different point of view.

One often hears the saying "nine out of ten people have hemorrhoids," showing that this has been a common complaint throughout the ages, and ancient China had many similar names for it — for example: mu zhi (male hemorrhoid), pin zhi (female hemorrhoid), mai zhi (vessel hemorrhoid), xue zhi (blood hemorrhoid), chang zhi (intestinal hemorrhoid), external hemorrhoid, internal hemorrhoid, the twenty-five hemorrhoids, the seventy-two hemorrhoids, and so on.

This is chiefly because the ancient concept of zhi (hemorrhoid) also encompassed several other growths such as nasal polyps ("nose hemorrhoids") and aural polyps ("ear hemorrhoids"), not only those of the anus and distal rectum. It must be noted that in both ancient and modern times, severe hemorrhoids belong to the domain of surgery, and modern surgical medicine is a trustworthy approach.

Traditional Chinese medicine's discussion of hemorrhoids mainly approaches the causes of their formation from the perspective of prevention and health cultivation. The principal patterns are as follows:

1. Large Intestine Excess Heat and Dryness-Heat

The Shanghan Zabing Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases) states: "When the small intestine has Cold, the person has rectal heaviness and blood in the stool; when it has Heat, hemorrhoids inevitably result." A fondness for heating (dry-hot) or spicy foods producing Excess Heat in the Large Intestine is a classic cause of hemorrhoid formation. In autumn, when the weather is dry and hot, external invasion by the Dryness-Heat pathogen also readily produces this pattern.

The symptoms are: severe pain around the anus; dry, hard, constipated stools (small pellets like goat droppings); flushed face and bad breath; insomnia and vexation; deep-yellow, scanty urine; dry mouth and tongue; a red tongue with little fluid and a yellow dry coating; and a floating-rapid or surging pulse.

In modern people the Triple Burner and Large Intestine meridians are energetically exuberant, so with improper diet and lifestyle habits, Large Intestine Fire arises very easily.

2. Damp-Heat accumulating and binding in the Large Intestine

When the weather is excessively damp and hot, Damp Qi invading the body can also generate Heat in the Large Intestine. Habitual dietary excess — eating too much, too fully, or too greasily, along with alcohol and spicy food — over time engenders internal Damp-Heat that accumulates and binds in the Large Intestine, gradually forming hemorrhoids.

The symptoms are: unsmooth passage of stool, tenesmus (urgency with rectal heaviness), abdominal distension, poor appetite, generalized heaviness and fatigue, a yellow greasy tongue coating, and a slippery rapid pulse.

3. Spleen Qi Deficiency with sinking of Middle Qi

Modern people, through chronic overthinking and overwork, develop Spleen Deficiency, leading to insufficiency of the body's Middle Qi. Excessive fatigue combined with prolonged standing or sitting causes the Middle Qi to sink; Damp-Heat then stagnates and accumulates in the Lower Burner, causing anal swelling and thereby precipitating hemorrhoid flare-ups.

Symptoms: a bearing-down sensation at the anus, weak ineffective straining at stool, shortness of breath and fatigue, poor appetite, a pale complexion, a pale tongue with white coating, and a deficient pulse.

For this type of hemorrhoid, one must first raise the ascending Yang Qi of the Spleen and Stomach in order to improve the hemorrhoids at their root.

4. Liver Qi constraint (Liver Qi stagnation)

Modern people face heavy work pressure, are prone to anger, and often stay up late, leading to Liver Qi stagnation and inhibited Qi dynamics. According to the zang-fu paired-communication (bie tong) relationship, the Liver and the Large Intestine communicate as a zang-fu pair — so when the Liver is unwell, the Large Intestine will not be well either!

The symptoms of this type of hemorrhoid are: proneness to anger and depression, intercostal pain after anger, chest oppression, abdominal bloating, poor appetite, and insomnia.

5. Qi stagnation and Blood stasis in the meridians

Prolonged sitting or standing causes poor movement of Qi and Blood in the buttocks and around the anus, forming hemorrhoids. In people with chronic constipation, Qi and Blood stagnate in the Lower Burner, which also causes hemorrhoidal swelling.

Modern people mostly sit for long periods, which frequently causes obstruction of the meridians around the buttocks. Meridian testing also shows that modern people exhibit Bladder meridian Deficiency whenever fatigued, and over time this leads to hemorrhoids.

Hemorrhoids refer to the pathological state in which the vascular tissue (cushions) of the anal canal becomes swollen or inflamed. According to statistics from National Cheng Kung University Hospital in Taiwan, the prevalence of hemorrhoids reaches as high as 86%.

The most common symptoms of hemorrhoids are painless bleeding with defecation (internal hemorrhoids), anal itching and burning sensations, anal discomfort or pain, and even prolapse of a mass from the anus.

The exact cause of hemorrhoids is unknown. The most common factor is poor circulation of Qi and Blood in the buttocks due to prolonged sitting or standing; and if prolonged sitting is combined with staying up late, smoking, heavy alcohol use, insufficient fiber and fluid intake, a fondness for spicy food, or chronic constipation, the risk of developing hemorrhoids is even higher.

Depending on location and type, hemorrhoids are classified as internal, external, or mixed. People with a history of ulcers, alcohol abuse and liver disease, or a smoking habit are also prone to hemorrhoids.

Modern medical treatment of hemorrhoids mainly involves topical ointments or simple outpatient procedures, such as rubber band ligation and electrocautery excision; severe hemorrhoids require conventional surgical excision.

For improving or removing hemorrhoidal tissue, modern medicine is already very mature. But for long-term prevention of hemorrhoids or their recurrence, the theories of Chinese medicine can be applied in conjunction.

Modern people sit for long periods, impairing the movement of Qi and Blood in the meridians of the buttocks.

Sleep disorders have unquestionably troubled the Chinese for well over a millennium, so from the time the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) was compiled there have been many similar names, such as: "eyes that will not close," "unable to sleep," "unable to lie down," bu mei (sleeplessness), "no sleep," "little sleep," "scant slumber," and other terms.

The basic model for understanding insomnia in Chinese medicine is this: because the ancients had no electric lighting, light was dim after about 7 p.m., so they fell asleep roughly between 9 and 11 p.m. and rose at 4 a.m.; inability to sleep during this period was called "insomnia."

Modern scientists have found that after 9 p.m. the brain's pineal gland begins secreting sleep-promoting melatonin, which fully explains that the ancients' sleep schedule was correct.

However, modern people generally fall asleep after midnight, and insomnia typically occurs between 1 and 4 a.m. — nearly the hour when the ancients were getting up. This point alone is already a cause of modern insomnia.

Modern people's sleep timing is simply wrong. The most central way to improve insomnia is to directly adjust the biological clock, or to use melatonin as an aid. If you can accomplish this, even the strangest and most intractable insomnia will completely disappear. It is truly a disease of modern civilization — and if that solves it, there is no need to read further!

If bedtime is normal yet insomnia persists, one can observe TCM patterns combined with meridian phenomena. Because so many Cloud TCM members suffer insomnia, related cases are extremely numerous, and the following 7 types have been summarized:

1. Sequelae of external Cold Damage: exuberant Yin with Yang failing to enter Yin; Spleen-Stomach Deficiency-Cold

The Shanghan Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage) is the classic text of the ages for treating "external Cold Damage," and it mentions the symptom of "inability to sleep" in many places — this can be described as a sequela left behind by colds.

Sure enough, since the global COVID-19 pandemic began in 2019, hundreds of millions worldwide have fallen ill, and the most common sequela has been insomnia. Many describe it as "utterly exhausted, yet simply unable to sleep" — which can be explained by Yin-Yang theory.

"Yin-Yang" is the most central theory in Chinese medicine; the entire system of Chinese medicine can be said to be constructed upon Yin-Yang doctrine. The Huangdi Neijing also states: "When pathogenic Qi lodges in a person, it may make the eyes unable to close and prevent lying down to sleep — what Qi causes this? ... Now when rebellious Qi lodges in the five zang and six fu organs, the defensive (Wei) Qi guards only the exterior, moving in the Yang and unable to enter the Yin ..." and "When defensive Qi cannot enter the Yin, it remains constantly in the Yang."

The contemporary renowned physician Dr. Zhang Cixing once said: "Daytime belongs to Yang, night belongs to Yin; when Yin and Yang Qi flow through, one can sleep peacefully." The moment Yang Qi enters the Yin meridians, a person becomes sleepy; the instant it leaves the Yin meridians, the person wakes. If the body's Yin and Yang are not in harmony, "Yang failing to enter Yin" is the chief cause of modern insomnia!

However, in many people, after COVID-19 vaccination or infection with the COVID-19 virus, the body's meridian pattern becomes like the one below: the energy of the Yang meridians is severely insufficient, presenting a "Yang Deficiency phenomenon." This is the classic insomnia-producing meridian pattern.

When Yin is exuberant and Yang is debilitated in the body, insomnia readily appears.

The Cloud TCM meridian testing system provides Yin-Yang values. Large volumes of modern meridian data show that in 75% of cases the Yin-Yang ratio is "Yin greater than Yang" — that is, modern people have as high as a 75% probability of insufficient Yang Qi (Yang-Deficient constitution), with Yin and Yang out of harmony.

With Yin Qi exuberant and Yang Qi insufficient, Yang failing to enter Yin, various sleep disorders naturally form! It may be said that of the diseases and symptoms troubling most modern people, many are caused by a Yang-Deficient constitution (exuberant Cold Qi).

The meridian chart above is from the younger sister of member Ms. Z, who developed a sleep disorder after the Beginning of Winter in 2019. She was clearly exhausted yet could not sleep, slept shallowly and woke easily, felt unrefreshed the next morning, and was drowsy during the day. This troubled her greatly; overall she felt gloomy and dejected.

After meridian testing, it was evident that the Yang meridian energy of her hands and feet was relatively insufficient. With the body's Yang meridian energy insufficient and Yin meridian energy in surplus, the "Yang failing to enter Yin" phenomenon described in the ancient books naturally presented itself — put simply, it was caused by Yang Deficiency.

Worth mentioning additionally: many modern people, from frequently eating cold-natured and icy foods, also often show this Yang-Deficient pattern — in plain language, "Spleen-Stomach Deficiency-Cold." This can be as simple as taking warming Chinese herbs (Fuzi Lizhong Tang / Aconite Center-Rectifying Decoction) together with warming physical therapies (such as a far-infrared sauna); once the abdomen and the Spleen and Stomach are warmed, it improves!

Combining massage of acupoints such as Sanyinjiao (SP-6), Shenmen (HT-7), Neiguan (PC-6), Yanglingquan (GB-34), and Zusanli (ST-36) gives even better results.

Insomnia caused by heavy internal Cold in fact has a similar etiology to depression, and likewise occurs with higher probability in women; readers may also consult the discussion of depression and its meridian relationships.

2. Deficiency above, Excess below: an extension of the Yang-Deficiency phenomenon

Insomnia caused by this internal Yang Deficiency appears in various transformed types. The most common is the variant of the "Cold-type Yang-Deficient constitution." There is one that does not look like a Yang-Deficient constitution but is in essence its variant — the "Deficiency above, Excess below" meridian pattern; a certain proportion of insomniacs show precisely this meridian phenomenon.

From the composition of "Deficiency above, Excess below" shown below, it is clearly formed from Deficiency of the three Hand Yang meridians — the classic Yang-Deficiency phenomenon. Judging from the meridians' pathways, one can say the entire abdomen is full of Cold; after this persists for a time, the entire chest also becomes obstructed, forming the Deficiency-above-Excess-below meridian pattern.

The Deficiency-above-Excess-below meridian pattern is in fact composed of two patterns.

In May 2022, a member with chronic insomnia found, after several meridian tests, that she presented the "Deficiency above, Excess below" meridian pattern. Since the probability of this pattern appearing in summer is very low — Yang meridian energy is strong in summer — it can almost be inferred that she shows this meridian phenomenon in all four seasons, pending continued observation.

Cloud TCM has many articles specifically discussing how the Qi and Blood of modern people's chests are frequently stagnant and obstructed, even producing the "Deficiency above, Excess below" meridian pattern; all of this can be improved through warming physical therapies combined with kneading the abdomen and massaging the relevant acupoints (click to read).

In June 2022, a member who had suffered continuous insomnia for 1-2 years reported that she showed precisely this meridian pattern. In the hot days of June she tested herself 10 times, and 8 of them showed Deficiency of the three Hand Yin meridians. Because she always woke at 3-5 a.m. and could not fall back asleep, a TCM physician prescribed Da Qing Long Tang (Major Bluegreen Dragon Decoction); after taking just one packet of the scientific herbal granules, she improved markedly.[@ad:1]

3. Chronic late nights producing the Iron Triangle meridian pattern

The above discussed insomnia caused purely by cold/flu sequelae, which is only one relatively probable cause. Another cause is also common: the series of internal "Yin Deficiency with Fire-Heat" phenomena produced by chronically staying up late.

Long-term observation of most Cloud TCM members has revealed that insomnia is a vicious cycle. Before insomnia develops, such people never liked to sleep — night owls staying up to work, watch films, or party; and to look energetic at night they love coffee, alcohol, and other stimulating drinks.

For years, such people exhaust themselves daily, holding on until the very last moment before finally sleeping. Testing the meridians of such a person mostly produces a chart like the one below — a chart resembling a "cocoon-spinning" process. Once this "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" appears stably, sleep is truly out of reach; one could call it "self-binding."

People who chronically stay up late naturally form this meridian pattern.

One female Cloud TCM member, about 47, began studying meridians precisely because of chronic insomnia. After testing herself more than 50 times, she confirmed clearly that her meridian chart stably showed Liver meridian Excess with Deficiency of the Spleen and Bladder meridians. She said: "I often cannot close my eyes the whole night — it is agonizing!"

She told the editor: "I used to have no idea what insomnia even was. I constantly watched YouTube deep into the night and got up after 6 a.m. — this went on for many years... and gradually... one day I truly could not sleep anymore!"

This meridian phenomenon also appears extensively in summer, which is why insomnia comes easily in summer. Observing people in whom other causes produce this meridian pattern, they too can hardly escape sleep disorders; this meridian pattern can thus be called the home base of insomnia.

On this basis, the cause of most people's insomnia is: at first you refuse to sleep; gradually, it is your body that will not let you sleep! This is both the cause of insomnia and its result.

When encountering this meridian pattern, the fastest method of improvement is "deep breathing, emptying the mind, relaxing the muscles." To improve the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern," the fastest route is thorough physical and mental relaxation. Once a person can truly relax, this meridian pattern begins to loosen; the great majority of people then start feeling sleepy all day and immediately escape the torment of insomnia.

Relaxation is always the most effective way to improve insomnia.

Some members have found that shortly after practicing yogic deep breathing or breath counting, although the mind becomes focused and calm, they promptly feel drowsy and sleepy — showing that most modern people are tense during the day, and it is the inability to relax that causes insomnia.

One insomniac member practiced relaxation methods diligently for three months and completely transformed the "Iron Triangle meridian pattern" causing his insomnia — even he found it hard to believe.

4. Iron Triangle variants: Liver-Stomach disharmony, Liver-Gallbladder constrained Heat, Heat harassing the chest and diaphragm

Continuing the previous case: this female member's insomnia was very severe. From January 2021 she went a full four months unable to sleep every night, a situation that continued for an entire year until February 2022. Her true meridian pattern was a variant centered on three meridians, and four key points must be grasped:

The meridian pattern of severe insomnia — four key points to grasp:

The Heart and Pericardium meridians show Deficiency, with frequent chest pain and chest oppression.

The Triple Burner and Large Intestine meridians are in Excess, indicating enormous accumulated internal Fire — too hot to sleep.

Liver meridian Excess with Deficiency of the Spleen and Bladder meridians — the self-binding "cocoon" pattern mentioned above.

Liver and Stomach meridians in Excess — Liver-Stomach disharmony, frequently accompanied by the Heat pattern of Gallbladder meridian Excess.

Besides her, other members have shared similar meridian phenomena. The common symptoms of this meridian pattern are: proneness to anger, impatience and irritability, dream-disturbed nights, unbearable feelings of body heat, frequent thirst, bitter or sour taste in the mouth (stomach acid), rib pain, dizziness, tinnitus, head distension, chest oppression and pain, easy hunger, abdominal and gastrointestinal bloating, indigestion, generalized aching, and so on.

Combined with traditional TCM patterns, this meridian pattern may correspond to "Liver-Stomach disharmony," "Gallbladder Heat," "Liver-Spleen disharmony," "Heart vessel stasis obstruction," "Yin Deficiency with effulgent Fire," "Heat harassing the chest and diaphragm," and so on — all chief causes of insomnia. Accordingly, some members have tried taking Jia Wei Xiao Yao San (Augmented Free and Easy Wanderer Powder) or Si Ni San (Frigid Extremities Powder); such Chinese herbs bring some degree of improvement, corroborating the ancient dictum "when the Stomach is not in harmony, sleep is not peaceful."

Some members have also found that on nights they cannot sleep, symptoms of body heat may in fact appear, such as vexation, chest oppression, nausea, bitter taste, and sour taste. Scientific herbal formulas that clear vexing Heat from the chest are also very effective, for example Zhuye Shigao Tang (Lophatherum and Gypsum Decoction) and Zhizi Chi Tang (Gardenia and Fermented Soybean Decoction).[@formula:202]

This corroborates traditional Chinese medicine's view that most insomnia is caused by excessive internal Heat. The Shanghan Lun states that febrile disease causes insomnia: through anger or stress, the Liver's capacity for free coursing becomes insufficient, and prolonged internal constraint transforms into Fire; or through alcohol and dietary irregularity, the Heat pathogen gathers in the Liver and Gallbladder, accumulates and transforms into Fire, and the Fire-Heat flames upward, disturbing the Spirit-brightness — the Heart Spirit is unquiet, hence insomnia.

5. Excessive pensiveness with Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency; chest stasis and obstruction

Having discussed Cold and Heat above, we turn next to the problem of "pensiveness." Chinese medicine often says "pensiveness damages the Spleen": people who habitually overthink develop a weakened Spleen — Spleen Deficiency.

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that when a person's Spleen Qi is weak, the source of Qi and Blood generation is insufficient; the Blood fails to nourish the Heart, and with Heart Blood insufficient, restlessness of the Heart Spirit readily appears — the so-called Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency.

Common symptoms are: insomnia, excessive dreaming with easy waking, pale complexion, fatigue and weakness, shortness of breath with little desire to speak, palpitations, forgetfulness, poor appetite, loose stools, a pale tongue with thin coating, and a thin, weak pulse.

Today meridian testing can clearly verify this phenomenon. The Cloud TCM development team is itself a group of people who use their brains all day. One software engineer among them uses his brain more than 10 hours daily; when he accumulated more than 200 meridian readings over a year and a half and plotted them as a single chart, it showed Spleen meridian Deficiency.

If this meridian pattern is further combined with prolonged sitting and excessive mental work, a meridian phenomenon resembling "Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency" readily appears. Engineers who work intensively with their minds are almost uniformly of this meridian pattern, so charts like the one below can easily be obtained from them:

A summer variant of the meridian pattern, frequently showing Deficiency of the Heart and Pericardium meridians.

The above is the meridian chart of one of those engineers, Mr. L. Whenever his work involves excessive mental effort, he frequently dreams excessively, wakes easily at night, readily feels dizzy and fatigued, gets short of breath climbing stairs, sometimes has palpitations and loose stools — and most noticeably, becomes especially forgetful.

He knows that the classic TCM formulas for improving Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency are Gui Pi Tang (Spleen-Restoring Decoction) or Ba Zhen Tang (Eight Treasures Decoction) — herbs that fortify the Spleen, boost Qi, nourish the Blood, and calm the Spirit. Whenever he begins overusing his brain, he makes sure to buy the scientific herbal granules and give himself a proper tonification.

By 2022 he reported that each time he finished a course of these tonifying herbs, his sleep clearly improved — evidence that the saying "pensiveness damages the Spleen" indeed holds true!

6. Heart and Kidney failing to communicate; exuberant Heart Fire

The contemporary renowned physician Chen Chao-tsung once said: "The problem of insomnia lies in the Heart." Chinese medicine accordingly has many insomnia diagnostic patterns related to the Heart, such as "Heart Yin insufficiency," "Heart and Kidney failing to communicate," "Heart Fire hyperactivity," and so on — all seeming to indicate that insomnia is related to the "Heart system" of organs (Heart, Pericardium, Heart meridian, Pericardium meridian).

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that when Heart Fire is exuberant, the Heart Spirit is unguarded, and there readily appear insomnia with excessive dreaming, vexing heat in the chest, palpitations, flushed face and bitter taste, thirst and dry mouth, sores of the mouth and tongue, a red tongue tip, and a rapid, forceful pulse. Because Heart Fire shifts its Heat to the Small Intestine, urine is scanty and dark, with painful, rough voiding.

This exuberant Heart Fire is often caused by insufficiency of Kidney Water: Kidney Yin cannot ascend to aid the Heart, Heart Fire blazes alone above and cannot descend to join the Kidney, and Heart and Kidney — Water and Fire — cannot assist each other; hence it is also called "Heart and Kidney failing to communicate."

Insufficient Kidney Yin producing effulgent Fire rests on the same principle, with symptoms of dizziness, tinnitus, tidal fever and night sweats, vexing heat in the palms and soles, forgetfulness and excessive dreaming, soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees, seminal emission, a red tongue with scant coating, and a thin, rapid pulse.

This abstract theory can actually be demonstrated with meridian data: large volumes of modern meridian data show that modern people have Heart meridian Excess and Kidney meridian Deficiency in all four seasons. Thus, for a certain proportion of people, their insomnia can be said with very high probability to originate here.

The meridian pattern of modern people: Heart meridian Excess and Kidney meridian Deficiency all year round.

Member Ms. S once shared that she occasionally has sleep disturbances. She frequently tests her own meridians: her Kidney meridian always shows Deficiency, and on careful observation her Heart meridian really does often show Excess!

Her sleep-disorder symptoms are difficulty falling asleep, vexation, occasional palpitations or chest oppression and pain, dream-disturbed nights, sometimes waking from vexing heat in the chest, and frequent dry mouth.

She recalled that once she sought treatment from a TCM physician, who prescribed Huanglian Ejiao Tang (Coptis and Donkey-Hide Gelatin Decoction), and it did clearly improve her sleep. She remembered the method of taking this medicine was unusual: the decoction was cooked and cooled, then a raw egg yolk was beaten into the liquid and stirred before drinking. Because she found this way of taking medicine uncomfortable, she stopped, and similar symptoms occasionally return.

7. Improving Excess-above-Deficiency-below insomnia is the hardest — and actually the simplest!

The final meridian pattern to mention is both the cause of insomnia and its result, making it the most difficult insomnia-producing meridian pattern to improve, especially in the middle-aged and elderly.

Modern medicine has found that the older one gets, the more prone one is to insomnia. Why? Meridian testing can supply numbers and images that could not be clearer. If one asks which insomnia is hardest to treat, the answer is the "Excess above, Deficiency below" meridian pattern.

In this state the meridian Qi and Blood permanently reside in the upper body; at night, even when the brain wants to close up shop, it cannot shut down, and one often counts sheep to the point of exhaustion before finally surrendering to sleep. In fact, this meridian pattern gradually evolves from each of the patterns above.

When the meridians present the Excess-above-Deficiency-below pattern, this insomnia is very hard to cure.

Most insomnia with no identifiable cause belongs to this type. And though this insomnia is the hardest to treat, it is actually also the easiest — because the Qi and Blood are excessively concentrated in the upper body, anyone who can guide the Qi and Blood downward will fall asleep in an instant. So it is in fact also the simplest!

There are many methods to improve upward-concentrated Qi and Blood. Some members have found through experiment that slow walking meditation before bed, guiding the Qi and Blood concentrated in the upper body downward, is very effective — during the day the whole body's Qi and Blood concentrate in the upper body, and people simply do not know how to guide them downward before sleep.

To fully slow the rapid-response thinking mode of the day before bed, the simplest method is to practice "walking meditation," observing the sensation of the feet contacting the ground; this guides Qi and Blood downward very quickly.

The chief reason a person's mental activity concentrates in the upper body is continued thinking before bed, which makes Qi and Blood float upward — and playing with one's phone before bed is the main culprit.

Light affects the human circadian rhythm. American medical research has found that using a tablet for just 2 hours each night suppresses melatonin secretion, impairs sleep quality, and lengthens the time needed to enter deep sleep. Which modern person does not use a phone before bed? Poor sleep is then only to be expected.

Looking at computers and phones before bed readily leads to insomnia.

Today's computer and phone systems can all enable night/dark mode, and everyone who must use a computer is advised to set it. Likewise, as with the previous point, modern people already overthink during the day, causing Qi and Blood to float upward; continuing to use the brain at night does nothing to help sleep quality!

Modern research has found that vigorous exercise within 3 hours of bedtime stimulates growth hormone secretion and raises metabolism; in some people the sympathetic nervous system becomes overactive and the brain has difficulty entering the sleep state, leading to insomnia — another contributing cause.

Taking all the above meridian patterns together, it is clear that the causes of insomnia are complex. But simply find your own meridian pattern, improve it, and keep observing — the insomnia will disappear naturally. It is really not difficult at all!

Insomnia is a very common symptom that troubles modern people. It refers to difficulty falling asleep, or waking mid-sleep and being unable to fall asleep again, or inability to achieve deep sleep, so that one still does not feel rested upon waking.

According to Western data reports, nearly 50 to 70 million Americans have experienced sleep disturbances. According to statistics from the Taiwan Society of Sleep Medicine, one in five people in Taiwan suffers from insomnia. National Health Insurance database statistics show that the number of people with insomnia in Taiwan is climbing year by year, with far more women than men — women outnumber men two to one.

The causes of insomnia are extremely numerous: stress (work, relationships, interpersonal issues, major life events, etc.); anxiety with an overactive mind preventing sleep; environmental factors (light, noise, changes in sleep environment, etc.); illness; consuming too much caffeine before bed; eating too much at night; poor sleep habits; a pillow that is too high; weather too cold or too hot; drug side effects; shift work; hormonal changes of menopause in women — and many more!

Insomnia may be short-term or long-term, and is generally accompanied by other symptoms: daytime fatigue and sleepiness, irritability, depression or anxiety, poor concentration, inability to focus on work, worsening memory, headaches, gastrointestinal discomfort — and gradually, worry begins as bedtime approaches.

Chronic insomnia triggers many further diseases, for example: depression, anxiety disorders, hearing problems (tinnitus, deafness), obesity, memory decline, skin diseases (dry skin, acne, dark spots, etc.), gastrointestinal diseases, lowered immunity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, and various cancers — it can be called a classic root of a myriad diseases.

Many diseases also conversely cause insomnia, for example: depression, anxiety disorders, rhinitis, fibromyalgia, arthritis, headaches, stomach pain, angina, diabetes, nocturia, and so on.

In recent times it has been found that sleep may be related to melatonin: as bedtime approaches, the brain begins to secrete melatonin, which peaks in the middle of the night, and its concentration gradually declines before morning waking.

Disordered circadian clocks are the chief cause of insomnia in modern people.

Modern people are frequently exposed to electric lighting, mobile phones, and computers, disordering the body's melatonin secretion and destabilizing the biological clock — this is likely the chief reason modern people are troubled by insomnia.

Modern medications for insomnia mainly use benzodiazepine hypnotics, which besides sedative-hypnotic effects also have anxiolytic, muscle-relaxant, and anticonvulsant actions. Non-benzodiazepine drugs, melatonin, antidepressants, antihistamines, and relaxants are also used for improvement.

Insomnia chronically troubles a certain proportion of people, and some do not wish to depend on sleeping medication long-term; insomnia can be understood from the perspective of Chinese medicine, offering another new line of thinking.[@ad:1]

Migraine, too, is a symptom that has troubled the Chinese for well over a millennium, so the ancient classics contain many similar names for it. This type of headache tends to be rather stubborn and not quickly cured; therapeutically it can be discussed together with ordinary "headache."

Holding a bronze acupuncture figure in hand, one can clearly see that the head is chiefly influenced by the Bladder meridian, while the meridian influencing the side of the head is principally the Gallbladder meridian. However, several other meridians — the Triple Burner, Small Intestine, Large Intestine, and Stomach meridians — also exert influence.

The Gallbladder meridian spreads across the entire side of the head.

The ancient text Lanshi Micang (Secret Treasury of the Orchid Chamber) states: "For pain in half the head, first take the Hand Shaoyang and Yangming, then take the Foot Shaoyang and Yangming — this is hemilateral headache (migraine)." This means headache is intimately connected with the Gallbladder, Triple Burner, Large Intestine, and Stomach meridians.

Long-term observation through meridian testing by Cloud TCM members has confirmed that migraine is indeed closely related to these 4 meridians, described in turn below:

1. Shaoyang meridian (Gallbladder and Triple Burner) abnormality

In modern people the Gallbladder meridian is Deficient in all four seasons, with a stable probability above 70%, higher in women than in men. The Triple Burner meridian is in Excess in all four seasons, with a stable probability of 60-70% or higher. It can therefore be said that the Shaoyang meridians of modern people are perpetually in an unbalanced, uncoordinated state.

Modern people's Shaoyang meridians (Gallbladder and Triple Burner) are chronically unbalanced.

If a person's Gallbladder meridian remains in severe Deficiency long-term while the Triple Burner meridian is in severe Excess, they truly can hardly escape the fate of migraine. In December 2021, a female member shared that her history of migraine exceeded 15 years; having begun meridian testing several years earlier, she found her Triple Burner meridian energy very high while her Gallbladder meridian was often very low.

Each migraine attack was accompanied by severe vertigo, aversion to cold, neck pain, low back pain or a cold sensation in the lower back, all-day fatigue and sleepiness, feelings of depression, tinnitus, a feeling of extreme internal dry-heat with an urge to snap at people in anger, aching arms, slightly blurred vision, and leg cramps — especially with a higher probability of attacks in winter. These are all classic symptoms of Gallbladder and Triple Burner meridian abnormality.

2. Yangming meridian (Stomach and Large Intestine) abnormality

The same situation occurs with the Yangming meridians. In modern people the Stomach meridian is Deficient in all four seasons with a stable probability of 50-60%, while the Large Intestine meridian is in Excess year-round, with a probability above 70% in summer. It can therefore be said that the Yangming meridians of modern people are perpetually in an unbalanced, uncoordinated state.

Modern people's Yangming meridians (Stomach and Large Intestine) are chronically unbalanced.

In November 2021, a male member shared that after winter began he developed facial muscle pain, pain on opening his mouth, and gradually a migraine. He found that both his Stomach and Large Intestine meridians showed Deficiency, with clearly insufficient Yangming energy.

When Yangming is abnormal, there can be olfactory disturbances, facial muscle abnormalities, shoulder and neck soreness, aching of the elbow and upper and lower arm, eye abnormalities, various Spleen-Stomach digestive-tract symptoms (constipation, diarrhea, poor appetite, persistent hunger, etc.), vertigo, disordered speech, and so on — all classic Yangming meridian symptoms.

3. Shaoyang and Yangming meridian variants

The above discusses the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians separately; in fact, on a single meridian chart they appear together. The Gallbladder and Stomach meridians are highly linked — when the Gallbladder meridian is Deficient, the Stomach meridian is Deficient in tandem — and the same holds for the Triple Burner and Large Intestine meridians, giving rise to the following two possibilities.

Common meridian patterns of the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians.

These two possible meridian patterns appear most readily in winter, becoming more pronounced the colder the weather gets — at which point the probability of migraine and its associated series of symptoms is very high!

4. The Liver-Yang-rising state

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that migraine appears with "Liver Yang rising" (ascendant hyperactivity of Liver Yang), with symptoms of distending headache, vertigo, dry eyes, tinnitus, vexation and irritability, sleep disturbance, rib-side pain, dry mouth and tongue, flushed face, a red tongue with scant coating, and a wiry or thin-rapid pulse. This is caused by emotional depression — Liver Qi constrained within the body for a long time transforming into Fire.

The Liver-Yang-rising meridian pattern readily produces migraine.

Some members have indeed observed this meridian phenomenon: the classic Iron Triangle meridian pattern plus Excess of the Shaoyang and Yangming meridians (as in the figure above). This genuinely does produce migraine, with a higher probability of appearing in summer, together with the series of Liver-Yang-rising symptoms — everyone can verify this for themselves.

Whatever the meridian pattern, long-term meridian obstruction in the body producing internal Qi stagnation and Blood stasis can give rise to migraine, because the meridians in which the human body most readily develops Qi and Blood stasis are the Bladder and Gallbladder meridians — and both of these meridians pass through the head.

From the above it is clear that external Cold most readily causes migraine, which is why migraine occurs most easily in winter. One can apply moxibustion, a hot hair dryer, or far-infrared irradiation to the head and the relevant meridian regions, or take a hot half-body bath, pat along the Gallbladder and Stomach meridians, and warm the navel — warming the abdomen is the fastest and simplest way to improve migraine.

The simplest method for improving migraine.
