Acne has unquestionably troubled the Chinese for over a thousand years. As far back as the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic), the formation of acne was discussed in detail. The Suwen (Plain Questions) of the Neijing states: 'When sweating meets dampness, acne and miliaria arise,' and 'When sweat from exertion meets wind, and cold thins it, facial blemishes form; when it stagnates, acne results.'

By the Sui dynasty, the Zhubing Yuanhou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Manifestations of Diseases) called it 'facial pao (face blisters).' The Qing-dynasty Yizong Jinjian (Golden Mirror of Medicine) called it outright 'Lung-Wind acne (fei feng fen ci),' and the Waike Dacheng (Great Compendium of External Medicine) also called it 'wine pimples (jiu ci)'; today it is commonly called 'fen ci' (comedones).

Later generations of Chinese medicine's views on acne can be summarized into the following five main possibilities:

1. Lung Heat readily produces skin diseases

Chinese medical theory holds that 'the Lung governs the skin and body hair.' Once the Lung channel is disordered, many skin diseases naturally appear, and acne is the most typical example. The main symptoms are facial itching, eruption of comedones accompanied by redness, swelling, and pain, along with dry mouth and parched tongue, a red tongue body with a yellow coating, scanty deep-yellow urine, and a tendency to dry stools.

Another reason acne appears when the Lung channel is abnormal lies with the Large Intestine channel: the Lung and Large Intestine channels form an exterior-interior pair, and these two channels are highly linked.

So when the Lung channel is diseased, the Large Intestine channel becomes diseased as well. In the modern-population meridian data published by Cloud TCM, the Lung and Large Intestine channels show high linkage, turning to Excess in synchrony after May-June each year; when the Excess becomes too severe, Lung-Heat-related skin diseases readily appear.

The Lung and Large Intestine channels are highly linked, turning to Excess from May-June until the end of the year

2. Severe Stomach Heat (Yangming Heat) produces facial acne

The Stomach channel belongs to the Yangming; the other Yangming channel is the Large Intestine channel, and both ultimately run to the face — hence their close relationship with acne. The Lung-channel analysis above also shows the shadow of the Large Intestine channel; clearly the Large Intestine channel is inseparable from facial acne!

Facial acne often appears along the pathways of the Stomach and Large Intestine channels

Fire in the Stomach channel usually comes from what one eats — for example, large amounts of fried food, or late-night snacks — accumulating in the belly over time to create accumulated Heat in the Spleen and Stomach. Acne caused by Stomach Heat presents as follicular papules from which a whitish-pink oily substance can be squeezed, sometimes with blackheads.

From the figure above one can see that when the Stomach and Large Intestine channels are abnormal, these pimples often grow around the mouth and nose, because these areas are influenced by the Yangming channels; they sometimes appear on the back and chest as well, all of which lie on the channel pathways. Draining Fire from the Large Intestine can improve the Fire-Heat of the Yangming channels, which is why one school of health cultivators places great emphasis on 'clearing retained stool as a health method.'

Because it arises from Stomach Heat, symptoms readily include frequent hunger, bad breath, dry mouth and parched tongue, a strong craving for ice water, hard dry stools that are difficult to pass, a red tongue body, a thick greasy coating, and so on.

This phenomenon can be verified through meridian testing. In summer one frequently sees the chart below — the typical picture of internal Fire-Heat; when this kind of meridian chart appears, a few pimples often erupt on the face.

The meridian phenomenon in which facial acne frequently appears during spring and summer

3. Staying up late at night generates Liver Fire, and pimples pop out automatically the next day

Acne from exuberant Liver Fire is in fact the type most people have experienced. Most modern people keep the Liver channel in an Excess state, so a few extra late nights make the Liver-channel Excess more severe; once it flares out of control, Liver Fire is produced, giving rise to all manner of diseases, of which acne is a typical example.

Why does Liver Fire cause acne? There is a saying everyone has heard — 'the Liver and Gallbladder reflect one another (gan dan xiang zhao).' The Liver and Gallbladder channels stand in an exterior-interior relationship. If a person regularly stays up past 11 p.m., they are failing to rest during the circulation hours of the Gallbladder and Liver channels, and Liver-Gallbladder Fire naturally arises.

The Gallbladder channel's pathway includes the head and face — especially the entire head — so some people's pimples grow not only on the face but also on the scalp.

A certain member, Mr. J, stayed up late over a long period and found he could not grow his hair long, because many pimples grew on his head; whenever his hair got too long it became unbearably itchy. He found it strange — why did the pimples grow not on his face but on his scalp?

Gallbladder-channel Fire makes pimples grow even on the scalp

After more than 50 meridian tests it was confirmed that his Liver channel showed Excess over 90% of the time and his Gallbladder channel showed Deficiency over 85% of the time. With long-term Liver-Gallbladder channel imbalance, each additional late night readily produced various Liver Fire symptoms (see the detailed reading on Liver Fire symptoms) — growing pimples being merely one small symptom among them.

Because Chinese medicine often discusses the Liver together with the Kidney — long-standing exuberant Liver Fire eventually also produces 'Kidney Yin Deficiency' — one school of Chinese medicine practitioners holds that Kidney Yin Deficiency is likewise a cause of acne, and the Fire must be extinguished by enriching Water and tonifying the Kidney! [@ad:1]

4. Blood Heat, toxic Heat, and Blood stasis make pimples erupt all over the body

One school of Chinese medicine approaches acne specifically through Blood Heat. This school holds that acne arises because the body's Qi and Blood have long circulated poorly, or because negative emotions have been constrained within the body too long, producing Qi stagnation and Blood stasis.

When Blood stasis and constraint persist, they transform into Heat, and prolonged Heat transforms into toxin, so the acne develops pustules, often with red halos, swelling, and pain around them, a flushed complexion, and at times fever — and the acne becomes extremely difficult to cure.

Chinese medicine holds that for this type of acne, only cooling the Blood, resolving toxin, and invigorating the Blood to transform stasis can uproot the pimples at their source. In fact, the various 'strange pimples' caused by Blood stasis are quite common, though modern medicine finds them hard to comprehend.

A female friend, about 40 years old, of Cloud TCM member Ms. S had unexplained itching on her back lasting 5-6 years; examinations at all the major hospitals found no cause. Meridian testing showed severe Deficiency of the Bladder channel.

When Qi and Blood are obstructed throughout the body, pimples manifest along the Bladder channel

Ms. S thought at the time: 'Then let me do gua sha scraping and cupping for her!' After the treatment, roughly 30-50 dark pimples visibly erupted on her back — which could indeed be called severe stagnant sha.

Both were dumbfounded on the spot, never having seen such a phenomenon! A few days later the friend said: 'The itching on my back has actually improved by 80%,' to Ms. S's delighted surprise!

Over the following month, Ms. S performed gua sha and cupping for her another 3 times; by the final session there was no trace of dark pimples on her back and the itching had completely disappeared. Her friend prepared a large red envelope for her, and both were overjoyed.

The friend said: 'Thank you for relieving me of this symptom that troubled me for years and made my whole body feel wrong — now I truly feel wonderful!'

In the Chinese medical view, wherever the body's Qi and Blood fail to flow freely, stasis and toxins are everywhere; manifesting on the face they become acne, and they may just as well appear on any part of the body. This is in fact the fundamental principle behind 'gua sha and slapping therapy curing a hundred diseases,' and the famous physicians, ancient and modern, who have made their way in the world with this technique are truly not few!

5. Do not assume that a Yang-Deficient, Cold-natured constitution cannot grow pimples

Looking at the analyses above — if not Heat then Fire, or else Blood toxin — it seems Chinese medicine holds that facial pimples are almost always caused by excessive internal Heat, fully matching acne's appearance of 'redness, swelling, heat, and pain.' Yet if treating acne were that simple, how could anyone be troubled by it for a lifetime?

Here is a real case. A friend of member Mr. M came from a wealthy family and was troubled by acne long-term, starting in junior high school; treated continuously right up to his entry into the workforce, his face still broke out endlessly, the whole face like the surface of the moon — a battle against acne lasting decades!

During that battle he tried at least 5-6 Chinese medicine practitioners and 6-7 Western medical clinics, along with every strange and unorthodox school, and in the end still was not cured.

After joining as a member in mid-2019, Mr. M became very active with meridian testing. He had always assumed acne was caused by internal Fire-Heat, but after testing this friend at least 10 times, he could see no obvious signs of Fire-Heat at all.

Many people with long-unhealed facial acne actually have a Yang-Deficient, Cold-natured constitution

His friend's meridian charts forever and stably showed Deficiency of the Triple Burner (Sanjiao) and Large Intestine channels. He said: 'Judging by Cloud TCM's discussion in the article on drinking ice water, this is caused by excessive Cold in the abdomen' — which puzzled him greatly.

He asked his friend: 'Shall we run an experiment? If your acne comes from excessive internal Heat, then taking Fuzi Lizhong Tang (Aconite Center-Rectifying Decoction) would certainly make it worse, since it is a very hot herbal formula — and yet you seem well suited to this formula?'

The friend said: 'Which method available to the medical world have I not tried? One more failure makes no difference to me!' After taking Fuzi Lizhong Tang for 5 days, the pimples not only did not worsen but began to erupt more slowly.

The friend said: 'Strange — I actually feel my spirits have improved, and no Fire signs have appeared.'

Mr. M said that using an extremely hot formula like Fuzi Lizhong Tang to improve acne is often seen in Chinese medical books; had the meridian data not been so unambiguous, he truly would not have dared make such a suggestion!

If this direction is correct, it means the treatment direction of the previous decade or more had all been wrong. Mr. M then studied many more Chinese medical books and confirmed that acne can be eliminated by improving a Cold constitution — and people like this are truly not few!

Since pimples arise from the several constitutional types above, how should they be changed? The method is actually simple, summarized in the following key points:

Eat fewer foods that increase internal Fire-Heat: eat less of what is overly sweet, oily, spicy, or hot in nature — for example coffee (coffee is actually quite heating), chocolate, cocoa, fried chicken, french fries, butter and cream, smoked and grilled foods, and deep-fried foods — to avoid adding internal Fire-Heat and causing more severe acne.

Eat more fiber-rich foods: the Large Intestine channel is intimately bound up with facial diseases, and keeping bowel movements regular can prevent pimples — for example eating more carrots, various green leafy vegetables, enoki mushrooms, and bamboo shoots helps intestinal peristalsis. Drinking yogurt drinks regularly also helps keep bowel movements smooth.

Consume cooling, toxin-resolving herbal teas or foods: once it is confirmed the acne is not caused by excessive Cold in the abdomen, one may take herbal teas and foods that drain Liver Fire — teas such as cassia seed (juemingzi) tea, chrysanthemum tea, and honeysuckle (jinyinhua) tea; foods such as lemon, mung bean, winter melon, cucumber, watermelon, carrot, tomato, water spinach, spinach, bamboo shoots, and so on.

Do not drink alcohol: alcohol increases internal Dampness and Heat and will be of no help whatsoever in improving acne.

The same old advice — go to bed early: fall asleep before 11 p.m. whenever possible; 11 p.m. to 3 a.m. is the circulation time of the Liver and Gallbladder channels, and sleeping then regulates Liver-Gallbladder function.

Drink a cup of warm water upon rising in the morning: drinking warm water in the morning is a secret of 'nourishing upright Qi'; it can also clear retained stool, eliminate bad breath, and regulate the whole body's immune system.

Take Chinese herbal medicine appropriately: once it is confirmed that the facial acne is caused by Fire-Heat, herbal medicine works very quickly. These Heat-clearing, Blood-cooling, Dampness-eliminating, toxin-resolving herbs can wipe out a pimple the moment it emerges — for example Pipa Qingfei Yin (Loquat Lung-Clearing Drink), Tiaowei Chengqi Tang (Stomach-Regulating Qi-Guiding Decoction), Qingshang Fangfeng Tang (Upper-Body-Clearing Saposhnikovia Decoction), Huanglian Jiedu Tang (Coptis Toxin-Resolving Decoction), Puji Xiaodu Yin (Universal Relief Toxin-Dispersing Drink), Jiawei Xiaoyao San (Augmented Free Wanderer Powder), Huangqin Qingfei Tang (Scutellaria Lung-Clearing Decoction), Liuwei Dihuang Wan (Six-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill), and so on. The herbal solutions are very rich — please research them yourself or consult a Chinese medicine practitioner.

Acne is a common skin disease, also known as pimples, facial blemishes, comedones, blackheads, or folliculitis — the skin disease most detested by anyone who cares about their appearance.

Modern medicine regards acne as a disease of follicular inflammation. The most common type of pimple is called 'acne vulgaris,' while comedones are 'non-inflammatory acne.'

Acne generally appears in the form of comedones, papules, pustules, hard raised red nodules, and cysts, subsequently leaving scars. The harm acne inflicts is largely psychological — loss of self-confidence, dejection, and even suicidal tendencies.

Modern medicine has found that acne is most common in adolescents and young adults (ages 12-25); up to 85% of young people are troubled by acne to varying degrees, and in most people it gradually improves with age. Some people still develop comedones around age 40 or 50.

Modern medicine's understanding of acne centers on excessive sebum secretion forming comedones; abnormal keratinization at the follicular opening causing follicular obstruction; overgrowth of Cutibacterium acnes (the acne bacillus); and inflammatory reactions of the follicle and neighboring skin tissue.

Other causes of acne are chiefly hormonal disturbance: 'stress' and 'insufficient sleep' readily disrupt hormonal balance, which in turn affects pore keratinization and sebum secretion, making breakouts likely. Women also undergo hormonal changes during menstruation or the fertile phase of the cycle, and thus break out at those times as well.

Improper diet (high-calorie and high-sugar foods, dairy products containing hormones) likewise worsens the skin and promotes pimples. Using unsuitable skincare products or cosmetics, or incorrect skincare methods, makes breakouts even more likely.

Sweating in hot, stuffy conditions, dirty environments, and drug side effects can also cause acne. Constipation alters the intestinal environment, allowing harmful substances to accumulate in the body; long-term constipation also leads to pimples.

The face and chin are where comedones concentrate; the chest, back, shoulders, and even the upper arms sometimes cannot escape them either, although lesions in these areas are usually keratosis pilaris rather than comedonal acne in the usual sense.

Some people's long-standing acne has been cured through alternative therapies, of which Chinese medicine is a major branch; therefore, for acne that has long failed to heal, Chinese medical treatment may also be considered.

In antiquity, terms like the modern 'hyperthyroidism' or 'hypothyroidism' were not used, but there were similar diseases, such as 'ying liu (goiter tumor).' The symptoms of hypothyroidism lean toward what Chinese medicine calls the categories of 'xu lao (Deficiency taxation)' and 'xu sun (Deficiency detriment).'

Thyroid dysfunction is divided into hyperfunction and hypofunction — one could say these are the two faces of one Yin-Yang whole: hyperfunction belongs to Yang, hypofunction belongs to Yin, and modern medicine's symptom observations happen to accord with Yin-Yang theory as well.

Thyroid abnormality accords with the concept of Yin and Yang

Hyperthyroidism has unquestionably troubled the Chinese for over a thousand years. In antiquity it was called 'ying disease (goiter)'; ying is the general term for thyroid diseases. An ancient text says: 'Ying means to encircle — it wraps the throat at the neck.' Ying carries the sense of entwining, referring to the class of diseases with nodular swelling on both sides of the front of the neck.

Ying disease encompasses several diseases named by modern medicine, including simple goiter, thyroid adenoma, thyroid cyst, thyroid cancer, and thyroiditis. Traditional Chinese medicine divides ying disease into four kinds: Qi ying, flesh ying, stone ying, and ying abscess.

The ancients observed that this disease mostly results from abnormality of the 'emotions (qingzhi)': mental and emotional stress leads to Liver Qi constraint, and the abnormal Qi and Blood of the Liver channel manifests in the vicinity of the neck — usually belonging to patterns of Qi Deficiency, or Yin Deficiency with exuberant Fire.

The greatest problem of traditional Chinese medicine is that it expounds a pile of abstract theory; the classical language is obscure enough as it is, and even with a complete translation the abstract principles remain hard to grasp. Today, one can use meridian testing to observe directly the meridian patterns of hyperthyroid patients — is that not the most direct and easily understood approach?

Since hyperthyroidism is a constitutional state, in theory the possibility can be observed several years — even more than a decade — before hyperthyroidism appears; herein lies the value of preventive medicine. In 2018, 4 years before the hyperthyroidism diagnosis, the Iron Triangle meridian pattern appeared

At the same time she found her body very prone to unbearable heat, which she took to be a menopausal phenomenon.

Hyperthyroidism (abbreviated as 'jiakang' in Chinese) is a disease caused by an excess of thyroid hormone; it is an 'autoimmune' disease. Hyperthyroidism results from thyroid oversecretion; the converse is hypothyroidism.

The thyroid lies in the neck below the Adam's apple, a gland shaped like a butterfly; it is the endocrine gland with the broadest influence — the metabolism of every organ in the body is affected by the thyroid, including the heart, muscles, eyes, bones, skin, mood, and so on — so the causes and symptoms of hyperthyroidism are very complex.

Hypotension refers to blood pressure below the normal range, defined as: systolic pressure below 90 mmHg and diastolic pressure below 60 mmHg.

Since most people do not measure their blood pressure regularly, and hypotension carries no immediate danger, it is often overlooked, and this condition is not considered to have any seriousness.

Common symptoms of hypotension include: dizziness (in severe cases even fainting), blurred and dimmed vision, unexplained fatigue, weakness, poor concentration, palpitations, a racing heartbeat, nausea and vomiting, cold hands and feet or bodily coldness, and rapid, shallow breathing.

Some people feel severe vertigo when they stand up from squatting

Common causes of hypotension include:

Postural (orthostatic) hypotension: when posture changes — for example from sitting or squatting to standing — blood pressure drops suddenly, the blood supply to the brain becomes insufficient, and the symptoms above then appear.

Poor venous return: in people who exercise little, long-term poor blood circulation in the lower limbs lets blood pool within the veins; the blood returning to the heart decreases, causing hypotension.

Anemia: an insufficient number of red blood cells readily gives rise to the problem of hypotension.

Postprandial hypotension: common in the elderly — after a full meal, blood enters the digestive system and blood pressure falls.

Drug side effects: some drugs — for example antihypertensive drugs, diuretics, sedatives, and drugs for erectile dysfunction — may cause hypotension.

Pregnancy: pregnant women, with rising weight and increased blood volume, bear a greater cardiac load and may show symptoms of hypotension, which return to normal after delivery.

Other diseases: some diseases such as thyroid disease, diabetes, heart disease, and kidney disease may also cause hypotension.

The most common phenomenon is postural hypotension: the dizziness many people feel after squatting down and standing up is caused by postural hypotension.

When a person goes from a sitting or squatting posture to standing, blood pressure drops suddenly, the blood supply to the brain becomes insufficient, and symptoms such as dizziness, dimmed vision, blurred vision, tinnitus, ear fullness and pain, nausea, vomiting, and even syncope may appear.

Modern medicine's research on hypotension is very clear; from the perspective of the meridians, another new line of thinking on hypotension can also be offered, which can prevent hypotensive phenomena.

'Cardiac arrhythmia' goes by many similar names; it refers to the various symptoms caused by abnormality of the heart's electrical conduction system. Under normal conditions, the human heartbeat is 60 to 100 beats per minute; if the heart's electrical conduction system is disturbed by any of various possible factors, causing the heartbeat to become too fast, too slow, or irregular, this is called 'arrhythmia.'

With technology advancing by the day, everyone today can determine within one minute whether they have an arrhythmia through a smartwatch or a downloaded phone app; those interested may tap to download [RhythmCam] (iOS/Android).

Since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, arrhythmia has been a topic of general concern, because when sudden death occurs in young and middle-aged adults, the most likely cause is 'arrhythmia.' About 1-2% of people experience arrhythmia, and the probability rises to 5-10% in those over 65.

Using a phone app to check for arrhythmia

About 80% of arrhythmias are benign, and most people are unaware of them; however, 20% are malignant — a form of heart disease prone to producing thrombi — and the stroke probability of such people is 5 times that of the general population.

Many arrhythmias present without symptoms; when symptoms occur, 'palpitations' appear — a sudden awareness of the heart's beating and pounding. Severe arrhythmias produce: chest tightness, chest pain, difficulty breathing, cold sweats, low blood pressure, dizziness, syncope (feeling about to faint), panic disorder, and so on.

The causes of arrhythmia are many, for example: heredity, excessive smoking and drinking, drinking coffee, heavy stress, electrolyte imbalance, drug abuse or side effects, diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea, hypertension, thyroid hypofunction or hyperfunction, coronary artery heart disease, and so on.

Most arrhythmias can be improved simply through a regular daily routine. Modern medicine employs antiarrhythmic drugs (for example: sodium, potassium, and calcium ion antagonists, beta-adrenergic blockers), or 'catheter ablation therapy'; some people have a pacemaker implanted.

Chinese medicine's view of arrhythmia proceeds by analysis from abstract concepts such as meridian Qi and Blood and cold-heat, which modern medicine can scarcely comprehend. If, after the various treatments of modern medicine, a person's results remain poor — or one directly wishes to choose an alternative therapy — one may then consult Chinese medicine's treatment theories.

Urinary frequency has troubled most Chinese people for the past thousand years and more, so classical Chinese medical texts contain a great deal of discussion of it; the ancients called it xiao bian shuo (frequent urination), long (dribbling urinary block), sou shuo (frequent voiding), xiao bian chou shuo (thick, frequent urine), and other such terms.

From the Chinese medical viewpoint, urinary frequency can be understood through the concept of the Triple Burner (San Jiao). The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic (Su Wen) states: 'The Triple Burner is the official of the sluices; the waterways issue from it,' indicating that the Triple Burner is the principal channel for the movement of body fluids and is closely connected with urination.

Since the Triple Burner is divided into Upper, Middle, and Lower Burners, problems in any of the three can produce urinary abnormalities.

The Upper Burner contains the Heart and Lung; the ancients held that Lung disorders can cause urinary frequency. The Middle Burner contains the Liver, Gallbladder, Spleen, and Stomach; the ancients mainly held that, since the Spleen governs the transformation and transportation of fluids, people with Spleen Deficiency are prone to frequency.

The Lower Burner contains the Kidney and Bladder — the part that most directly affects the urinary system. The Inner Classic states: 'When the water-spring does not cease, the Bladder is failing to store,' proposing that urinary frequency is intimately related to the Bladder fu-organ; hence people with Lower Burner problems are prone to frequency.

Taken together, urinary frequency reflects poor regulation and distribution of fluids by the zang-fu organs. Chinese medicine holds that the organs most directly involved in the body's fluid regulation are the Lung, Spleen, Kidney, and Bladder.

On this basis, the patterns associated with urinary frequency become relatively easy to understand, set out as follows:

1. Externally contracted Cold Damage affecting the Lung and Spleen

The Treatise on Cold Damage (Shang Han Lun) is the definitive text of the ages on treating externally contracted Cold Damage, and it mentions the symptom of 'inhibited urination' in many places.

Viewed from the Triple Burner, a common cold or Cold Damage necessarily affects the Lung and the Spleen-Stomach, thus involving the Upper and Middle Burners and producing urinary disturbance.

Externally contracted Cold Damage affects the Lung and the Spleen-Stomach digestive system.

The first formula to mention is Wu Ling San (Five-Ingredient Powder with Poria), which treats inhibited urination in Taiyang disease. It can be called a divine formula of the ages: it works very well for both absent urination and frequency, exerting a bidirectional regulatory effect!

Physicians ancient and modern have regarded this as the 'Taiyang water-amassment pattern,' caused by impaired Bladder Qi transformation, but modern scholars have found on studying it (Note 1) that, judging from the composition of Wu Ling San, it should rather be Cold Damage affecting the Lung and Spleen and causing obstruction of the Triple Burner; it is the foundational formula for regulating the body's fluid-metabolism system.

This inference is entirely reasonable. Quite a few Cloud TCM members have long-standing Spleen channel Deficiency patterns. Members frequently report that whenever there is heavy rain outside, they begin to experience urinary frequency, because the rise of Dampness in the body impairs the Spleen's transformation function.

More importantly, some of them took Wu Ling San at once, and this urinary frequency truly did improve very quickly.

2. Spleen Deficiency (Spleen Qi Deficiency, Spleen Yang Deficiency) causing Water-Qi disease

Continuing from the Spleen Deficiency mentioned above: it is not necessarily caused by a cold. Modern habits of staying up late, overusing the brain, and frequently drinking iced water also produce Spleen Deficiency.

The ancients held that Spleen-Deficient people develop urinary frequency. Large volumes of meridian data from modern people show a high probability of 'Spleen channel Deficiency patterns,' which also demonstrates that modern people very easily become Spleen Deficient.

Because 'the Spleen governs transformation and transportation,' once the Spleen's capacity to transform and move water becomes insufficient, 'internal retention of water-rheum' appears and in turn causes urinary frequency.

Spleen Deficiency causes Water-Qi disease, with urinary frequency as one symptom.

Simply put, urinary frequency is one symptom of 'Water-Qi disease' (a disorder of water transformation and movement); other symptoms include dizziness, palpitations, cough and wheezing, chest oppression and shortness of breath, thirst, edema of the four limbs, reduced appetite, a pale tongue with a white greasy or white slippery coating, a wiry-slippery pulse, and so on.

This Spleen-Deficiency type of frequency is similar to the patterns Chinese medicine commonly calls 'Liver Qi stagnation,' 'Middle Qi insufficiency,' and 'Spleen-Stomach Deficiency-Cold,' because all of these patterns include Spleen Deficiency; only the herbs used to improve them differ.

Some people develop frequency the moment they drink iced water or eat watermelon; this too results from cold-natured foods producing 'Spleen-Stomach Deficiency-Cold.' In short, Spleen-Deficient people are prone to urinary frequency.

Each year after autumn and winter set in, 'Water-Qi disease' flares easily, which suffices to explain why urinary frequency so readily appears after autumn and winter.

Moreover, the 'Iron Triangle meridian pattern' that frequently appears in summer is precisely a Spleen channel Deficiency pattern. One member reported in July 2024 that he had urinary frequency even in the hot summer, and his meridian chart clearly showed Spleen channel Deficiency.

A male Iron Triangle meridian pattern, with frequent urinary frequency.

Besides frequency, he was also often constipated, had developed skin disease, and had the thirst that frequently accompanies water-metabolism disturbance — all very typical of such cases.

The Treatise on Cold Damage says: 'If he wishes to drink water, give it to him little by little, so that the Stomach Qi is harmonized and he recovers.' It turns out that drinking water in small sips can actually be used to treat disease!

Some members have also found that they feel thirsty all the time, yet want to urinate immediately after drinking, as if the water were not absorbed at all — a typical symptom of Spleen-Kidney Qi and Blood weakness. People in this situation should not gulp water in large mouthfuls; small sips quench thirst just as well while reducing the frequency.

3. Lung Deficiency (Lung Qi Deficiency, Spleen-Lung Qi Deficiency)

Viewed through the Five Phases, Spleen Deficiency essentially entails Lung Deficiency: the Spleen-Stomach belongs to Earth and the Lung to Metal; when the Spleen-Stomach is weak, Earth cannot generate Metal, and Lung Deficiency naturally follows. Hence formulas that treat Lung Qi Deficiency ordinarily contain Spleen-Stomach herbs.

From the meridian perspective, when Spleen Qi fails to ascend, it cannot disperse essence-Qi to the Lung. So a person whose Lung is unwell is also prone to urinary frequency.

People with Lung disease also develop urinary frequency.

And usually, when a person's Lung is unwell, it began with externally contracted Cold Damage that was not properly resolved — which brings us back to the external contraction discussed at the very top.

When a person's Lung is weak, besides frequency there are other symptoms as well, for example: shortness of breath, sneezing, itchy nose, nasal discharge, loss of smell, constipation, palpitations, copious white phlegm, aversion to drafts, chest oppression, cough and wheezing, a pale tongue with white coating, and a weak pulse.

This explains why Ma Huang Jia Zhu Tang (Ephedra Decoction plus Atractylodes), a Chinese formula that treats the Lung, can also improve urinary frequency.

4. Bladder Deficiency-Cold and Damp-Heat

The discussion so far has essentially concerned the Lung and Spleen, but urinary frequency is of course related to the Bladder itself. The ancients found that both 'Bladder Deficiency-Cold' and 'Bladder Damp-Heat' cause urinary frequency.

Whether the Kidney-Bladder is Deficient-Cold or Damp-Hot, urinary frequency appears.

In 'Bladder Deficiency-Cold' frequency, the urine is clear, copious, and watery, accompanied by mental fatigue, soreness and weakness of the lumbar region and knees, aversion to cold and chilliness, edema of the lower limbs, a pale tongue with white coating, and a deep, thin pulse.

'Bladder Damp-Heat' frequency resembles urethritis and appears most readily in summer, produced by the hot and humid summer weather. The symptoms are: urinary urgency, painful urination, a burning sensation in the urethra, scanty dark-yellow urine, lower-abdominal distension and fullness, dry mouth and thirst, constipation, a red tongue with a yellow greasy coating, and a slippery, rapid pulse.

The Kidney and Bladder stand in an interior-exterior relationship. Although frequency manifests as disease of the Bladder, its source lies in the Kidney: it is the result of insufficient Kidney Qi with disordered Qi transformation, which produces the Bladder problem.

Bladder problems must therefore be resolved together with the Kidney. The ancients held that Kidney Deficiency (Kidney Qi Deficiency, Kidney Yin Deficiency, Kidney Yang Deficiency) produces frequency, accompanied by dizziness, tinnitus, sleep disturbance, soreness and weakness of the lumbar region and knees, hard stools, cold hands and feet, easy fatigue, and so on.

Large volumes of meridian data from modern people also corroborate the relationship between Kidney channel Deficiency and frequency; one of the meridian phenomena most commonly seen in modern people is Gallbladder channel plus Kidney channel Deficiency.

One member reported in April 2024 that she often had tinnitus and urinary frequency, with sleep disturbance at night; this meridian phenomenon could be seen clearly on her chart.

People with Kidney channel Deficiency are very prone to urinary frequency.

Using Chinese herbs to improve Kidney-Bladder Deficiency-Cold and raise Kidney Qi can improve frequency. The most commonly used formula is Ba Wei Di Huang Wan (Eight-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill), whose effect has remained stable through a thousand years of use.

The renowned physician Zhang Bu-Tao wrote in his book Ingenious Explanations of Zhang Bu-Tao's Prescriptions: 'For frequency so severe that in winter one must get up seven or eight times in a night, Shen Qi Wan (Ba Wei Di Huang Wan) can of course take effect!'

Note 1: Cheng Kai, et al. 'A Re-analysis of the Wu Ling San Pattern in the Treatise on Cold Damage.' Guiding Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine and Pharmacy 27.11 (2021).

The side effects of certain medications can also cause urinary frequency, for example: calcium channel blockers, diuretics, lithium, SSRIs (used to treat depression), antibiotics, and so on.

The causes of urinary frequency are extremely complex. When frequency is not caused by the diseases above, it is very well suited to the application of Chinese medical theory, which provides a new alternative line of thinking.

Nocturnal frequency/polyuria has indeed troubled the Chinese for more than a thousand years. As early as around 600 CE, the classical text Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Manifestations of the Various Diseases) clearly recorded: 'Copious, uninhibited urination arises from Bladder Deficiency-Cold and slipperiness of the bladder. The Kidney is the zang; the Bladder is the fu of the Kidney; as exterior and interior they both govern water. Kidney Qi passes downward to the genitals; since the fu is Deficient-Cold and cannot warm its zang, the urine is white and copious; and when nocturia is especially severe, it is because internal Yin Qi is arising.'

The meaning of this passage is that frequent urination is caused by 'Bladder Deficiency-Cold.' The Bladder is the organ attached to the Kidney; the two stand in an interior-exterior relationship, and both govern water.

Kidney Qi travels downward to the genital region; since the Bladder is Deficient-Cold, it cannot warm the Kidney, so the urine is white and copious. If nocturia is especially heavy, it is because the internal 'Yin-Cold Qi' is exuberant.

Thus the ancients held that Bladder Deficiency-Cold denotes insufficiency of the Bladder's Yang Qi, which leads to urination that is hard to control and therefore frequent. Nocturia is especially heavy because Yang Qi is weaker at night and the Bladder is more easily affected by Cold.

The ancients held that Yin-Cold of the Kidney and Bladder is the cause of urinary frequency.

The following are some common symptoms of frequent urination:

A marked increase in the number of urinations, with frequent trips to the toilet both day and night.

A relatively small urine volume, with clear, transparent urine.

Urination that is hard to control, with a tendency to urinary incontinence.

A cold sensation in the lower abdomen, with lumbar soreness and back pain.

On this basis, nearly all Chinese physicians of later generations have continued to use this concept when diagnosing nocturnal frequency. The Kidney governs Water and controls opening and closing, while the Bladder governs the storage of urine; hence nocturnal polyuria is inseparable from the Kidney and Bladder of Chinese medicine.

Daytime is 'Yang' and nighttime is 'Yin'; at night Yin flourishes and Yang wanes. Nocturnal polyuria is therefore the result of weak Yang Qi.

Explained in a single sentence: frequency/polyuria, whether by day or by night, is caused by insufficiency of the Yang Qi of the Kidney and Bladder.

In November 2023 a member shared that after autumn and winter arrived, the frequency of his nighttime urination clearly increased: previously only once a night, it now reached twice, each time with a large urine volume of clear, transparent urine — even though he had not drunk much water before bed.

Having performed meridian testing on himself for 3 years, he had confirmed that he belongs to the 'Cold-type Yang-Deficient meridian constitution,' and it is like this every year when winter comes.

He said: 'Actually it is not only in winter. Even in summer, as long as I stay in an air-conditioned room where the temperature is too low, I immediately become very frequent, especially from the afternoon onward.'

The so-called 'Cold-type Yang-Deficient meridian constitution' commonly presents Deficiency of the Gallbladder, Stomach, and Kidney channels, or Gallbladder plus Kidney channel Deficiency, just as in the figure below — this is the meridian pattern most prone to frequency/nocturia.

The most common meridian pattern of the Yang-Deficient constitution.

From the figure above it is easy to see that in cold weather — that is, when the temperature drops — the probability of this meridian pattern appearing rises, fully corroborating the ancient theory of Chinese medicine.

So even without performing meridian testing on oneself, this meridian phenomenon appears in most people, which is why the probability of frequency/nocturia in winter is higher than in summer.

Besides this Yang-Deficient meridian pattern, another common pattern, the 'Iron Triangle,' can also produce frequency/nocturia.

One member who observed her own meridians long-term confirmed that she belongs to the 'Iron Triangle' meridian constitution; she experienced frequency/nocturia nearly every night, which often affected her sleep.

A large proportion of people with the Iron Triangle meridian pattern very readily show the phenomenon of 'Kidney channel Deficiency.' This meridian pattern consists of Spleen channel Deficiency together with Kidney and Bladder channel Deficiency — which of course means insufficient Kidney/Bladder Qi and Blood, no less serious than the Yang-Deficient meridian phenomenon.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern can also present Kidney channel Deficiency.

This is why the ancient Chinese physicians discovered that 'Liver constraint with Blood Deficiency,' 'Spleen Deficiency with exuberant Dampness,' 'Liver-Kidney insufficiency,' 'Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency,' 'Spleen-Kidney dual Deficiency,' and the like can also cause frequency/nocturia — something meridian data can fully corroborate.

Accordingly, the treatment methods for improving nocturia begin to grow complicated: it is no longer as simple as treating only 'Kidney Deficiency' or 'Cold'!

A certain proportion of people have a meridian constitution tending toward the 'composite meridian constitution' — some Iron Triangle features plus some Cold — so Kidney channel Deficiency is a certainty, and they can hardly escape the trouble of frequency.

People with nocturia usually also have other concurrent symptoms, for example: dizziness, depression and fatigue, tinnitus, hearing impairment, lumbar soreness and back pain, seminal emission, premature ejaculation, knee pain, diarrhea, cold limbs, poor appetite, and so on.

Whatever the cause of the Kidney Deficiency, proper health cultivation that raises the energy of the Kidney channel will improve nocturia symptoms. For those with heavy internal Cold, simply expelling the Cold, boosting the body's Yang Qi, and keeping the body warm will improve frequency/nocturia.

Those who overuse their brains, are excessively fatigued, or are under too much stress should start with relaxing body, mind, and spirit, combined with taking some Chinese herbs that harmonize the Liver, Spleen, and Kidney, which can fundamentally improve frequency/nocturia.

Once one finds one's own cause and cultivates health accordingly to improve the abnormal meridians, long-troubling frequency/nocturia will improve — everyone can verify this personally.

'Nocturia' is a condition that compels a person to wake at night to urinate. Waking once during the night to urinate is common for most people, but more than 2 times is not a normal phenomenon and severely disrupts nighttime sleep.

Nocturia mainly comprises two situations, 'nocturnal urinary frequency' and 'nocturnal polyuria': nocturnal frequency refers to how often one urinates, while nocturnal polyuria refers to the volume of urine; a large nighttime urine volume is not a normal state.

In both men and women, the incidence of nocturnal frequency correlates positively with age: the incidence is about 20% at ages 20 to 40, about 60% at 60 to 80, and about 80% over age 80 — the older one is, the more readily this phenomenon appears.

There are many causes of nocturnal polyuria, and ambient temperature is often the main one. When temperatures fall in winter, the body sweats less and water cannot be expelled through the sweat glands; in addition, low temperature stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and the urethral sphincter contracts, so urination naturally becomes more frequent.

Urinary frequency and polyuria readily occur in cold weather.

Furthermore, hormonal imbalance and reduced bladder contractility are often primary causes. During sleep the body secretes 'antidiuretic hormone,' which reduces urine volume and concentrates the urine; if nighttime urine volume remains very large, it is usually because antidiuretic hormone secretion is insufficient.

In men, prostatic hyperplasia reduces bladder capacity and increases nocturia. In women, urinary tract infection and inflammation cause urgency, nocturia, and related symptoms. Some people have frequency or polyuria throughout the day, which may be caused by an underlying disease, for example: diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, or polydipsia.

In some people the nocturnal frequency is spurious and is in fact a 'sleep disorder': while tossing and turning in bed, they become especially sensitive to the urine in the bladder, and even a tiny amount must be voided before they can fall asleep at ease. Thus nocturia causes sleep disturbance, and sleep disturbance in turn causes nocturia.

The most direct way to improve nocturia is to change lifestyle habits, for example: within 4 hours of bedtime, minimize water, tea, coffee, alcohol, fruit, and the like, and develop the habit of emptying the bladder before sleep. Sit quietly and relax before bed to improve sleep, exercise more to sweat, lose weight, keep warm while sleeping, and so on.

Modern medicine treats nocturia with medications, commonly including: diuretics, antidepressants, female hormones, vasopressin, antihistamines, and others; for loss of bladder function, obstructing prostatic hyperplasia, bladder tumors, stones, or urethral stricture, surgery is used.

If a person has no related disease and simply has nocturnal frequency of unknown cause, the concepts of Chinese medicine are well worth consulting and can still markedly improve nocturnal frequency or polyuria.

Tinnitus has unquestionably troubled the Chinese for more than a thousand years. Ancient Chinese medical texts frequently discuss tinnitus and deafness together, because the causes underlying these two conditions are the same.

The ancient text Wai Ke Zheng Zhi Quan Shu (Complete Book of Patterns and Treatments in External Medicine) states: 'In tinnitus there is sound within the ear — sometimes like the chirping of cicadas, sometimes like the tolling of a bell, sometimes like the crackling of fire, sometimes like the sound of flowing water, sometimes like the winnowing of rice; or, when asleep, like the beating of war drums, like wind entering the ear.'

If tinnitus is examined through Chinese medical patterns, the possibilities are very numerous — at least a dozen or more. The simplest starting point is to begin by studying the meridians that pass through the ear.

Speaking of the ear, the first and most important meridian is the Triple Burner (San Jiao) channel, called the 'ear vessel' in antiquity — so it is evident that the ancients considered diseases of the ear necessarily linked to the Triple Burner channel.

Besides the Triple Burner channel, according to the meridian expert Lin Yun-Gui's Illustrated Guide to the Meridians, the channels reaching the ear also include the Gallbladder, Bladder, Small Intestine, Stomach, and Kidney channels and the Large Intestine luo-vessel — six channels and one collateral in all. Clearly the meridians reaching the ear are very complex.

Six channels and one collateral reach the ear in all.

Is the ear vessel really the Triple Burner channel? Many people do not know this, nor can they understand what the Triple Burner channel is.

Mr. K, a Cloud TCM member, once shared that through long-term observation of the relationship between his body and his meridians, whenever he feels internal Fire flaring, the area near Guanchong (TB-1) beside the ring-finger nail becomes painful, and tinnitus appears briefly for about 30 seconds before quickly disappearing; simply bloodletting at Guanchong to release the excess Fire makes the tinnitus vanish — reliably, every single time.

Another member, an acupuncturist long in practice abroad, also shared: 'Whenever a patient presents ear discomfort — a blocked ear, tinnitus, ear pain, and so on — needling Zhongzhu (TB-3), Yemen (TB-2), and Yifeng (TB-17) on the Triple Burner channel brings rapid improvement!' Clearly the Triple Burner channel is intimately bound up with the ear.

From antiquity to the present, Chinese medicine has had many methods of treating tinnitus, generating many pattern differentiations of great complexity; tallied up, they number at least a dozen or more (see figure below), dazzling to behold. A student of Chinese medicine who sees such a classification may well conclude that he will never be able to learn it!

The Chinese medical patterns of tinnitus/deafness/ear pain are quite complex.

Yet no matter whether the Chinese medical patterns causing tinnitus number in the hundreds, and the herbs treating it in the hundreds, the underlying meridian patterns number at most only 3-5, so the complexity can be entirely reduced to simplicity — it is not hard to learn at all! Some simple meridian patterns are summarized here:

1. The across-the-board Yang-Deficient meridian pattern

When a person has a Yang-Deficient constitution, the interior of the body is very Cold, and the meridian pattern that appears is often the state in the figure below: Deficiency of the Liver, Gallbladder, Stomach, and Kidney channels, with the Triple Burner and Large Intestine channels also showing Deficiency.

Simply put, in this meridian pattern the Shaoyang and Yangming channels are all Deficient; one can say the region leading to the ear is in a state of meridian obstruction all year round, so over time tinnitus very readily appears.

Many people previously could not read this meridian pattern; now, by simply opening 3D mode, it becomes very easy to understand. From the figure below one can see that the meridians leading to the area around the ear are all blue — a phenomenon of blockage.

The across-the-board Yang-Deficient meridian pattern most readily produces tinnitus.

This meridian pattern very readily appears in cold winter, and there is a good chance of patterns such as 'Liver Blood Deficiency,' 'Kidney Yin Deficiency,' 'Kidney Yang Deficiency,' and 'Heart-Kidney non-interaction' appearing — all of which may present tinnitus, accompanied by other symptoms.

In this meridian pattern the Liver channel is Deficient, and the Liver's function of storing Blood fails in its duty. The Kidney channel shows Deficiency in nearly all four seasons. The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic states: 'Kidney Qi communicates with the ear; when the Kidney is in harmony, the ear can hear the five tones. When the five zang are in disharmony, the seven orifices are not free' — so the ears will certainly not be normal.

Setting these patterns aside, it is more direct to understand it straight from the meridians: do these meridians not all pass through the ear? When these ear-traversing meridians all suffer insufficiency of Qi and Blood, of course tinnitus or hearing decline appears! Simply raise the energy of these Qi-and-Blood-deficient meridians, and the tinnitus will improve.

Chinese herbs can also be used to unblock the meridians. One member shared in 2020 that she developed tinnitus and ear pain, with even her throat and neck aching; she took a single dose of Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang (Ephedra, Aconite and Asarum Decoction) as concentrated scientific herbal granules, and to her surprise both the sore throat and the ear pain resolved.

In 2022 another member shared that after entering winter he would occasionally develop tinnitus. Since he has exactly this meridian pattern, he bought a far-infrared radiation device and, besides warming his feet, also warmed his hands and the side of his head; he felt the improvement was very distinct, and his previous cold hands and feet improved as well. [@ad:1]

2. Variants of the Iron Triangle meridian pattern

If a person with tinnitus consults a Chinese physician, the doctor will usually say it is a phenomenon of internal Fire-Heat, so in Chinese medicine tinnitus is very often diagnosed as a 'Heat pattern.' This direction is not wrong, and meridian data can corroborate it.

The heavy internal Cold phenomenon mentioned above appears in at most 30%-40% of people; not everyone's interior is Cold — in a certain proportion of people the interior is Hot.

The Iron Triangle meridian pattern in particular most readily produces Heat patterns. Once the Iron Triangle pattern has persisted for a period, an extreme-Heat phenomenon readily appears — that is, the meridian pattern in the figure below: the Shaoyang channels (Triple Burner, Gallbladder) and the Yangming channels (Stomach, Large Intestine) are all Excess, the Liver channel is Excess as well, while the Spleen and Bladder channels show Deficiency.

The Iron Triangle variant pattern readily produces tinnitus.

From the figure above one can easily see that the meridians around the ear are all red — a picture of blazing Heat — which makes tinnitus even more likely.

This meridian pattern very readily appears in hot summer, and the 'Wind-Heat' colds of summer also present a similar meridian phenomenon. This pattern may further present 'Liver Fire flaming upward,' 'ascendant hyperactivity of Liver Yang,' 'blazing Gallbladder and Stomach Fire,' exuberant internal Fire-toxin, and other such patterns, accompanied by various other symptoms.

A Cloud TCM member shared in July 2020 that she had developed tinnitus and ear pain — at first appearing once every 1-2 days and quickly vanishing; gradually it appeared once every day, and by August 3-5 times a day, making her very uncomfortable. During this period she frequently had dizziness, heat in the chest, irritability, dry mouth and tongue, constipation, poor sleep at night, poor appetite with inability to eat, and so on.

Abnormality of the meridians leading to the ear, causing tinnitus and ear pain.

From the chart one can see that her meridian pattern is the one commonly seen in summer, which carries a certain probability of tinnitus. Yet this meridian pattern can appear in all four seasons — through staying up late and heavy work stress.

In December 2022, in winter, a new member shared through the Facebook group that he had tested continuously for two weeks since early December, and the meridian charts were all very similar, with the Gallbladder channel Excess nearly every day.

What troubled him most was high-frequency tinnitus in the right ear for over a year, along with abnormal lymph nodes at the right jaw and a sore feeling in the cheek behind the right lower jaw — all of these located along the course of the Gallbladder channel.

The meridian pattern of a man with high-frequency tinnitus of the right ear persisting over a year.

This meridian pattern may very well also be a variant of the Iron Triangle pattern, merely hidden by testing in winter; with continued observation into May-June of the following year, the typical Iron Triangle phenomenon would usually appear.

Since this meridian pattern is quite difficult to resolve, and the diseases it produces go well beyond tinnitus, Cloud TCM has previously summarized it in an article (click to read) and proposed related solutions (click to read).

In fact, if you simply Google and learn from the experiences shared by people with chronic tinnitus, you will find common features, for example: fondness for staying up late, very heavy work stress, busy detail-laden work, a bad temper with quickness to anger, an overly perfectionist personality, jumpiness, and a neurotic, almost paranoid state all day long. Clearly, accumulated 'fatigue' and 'poor emotional states' are the most typical causes of tinnitus!

In many people, tinnitus pops out of its own accord when they stay up late; if at that moment you test your own meridians on the spot, you will see a similar meridian pattern. When this article was first being written, the editor developed tinnitus while writing late into the night, hurried off to sleep, and continued the next day.

3. Spleen-Stomach weakness

The two meridian patterns above have in fact fully explained the two extreme meridian patterns behind tinnitus; ordinary people do not reach such severe states.

Whichever of the two patterns is present, however, the 'Spleen-Stomach weakness' pattern readily appears, and at that point tinnitus also readily arises. This is because the Spleen-Stomach is the source of the generation and transformation of Qi and Blood; when the Spleen-Stomach is weak or Spleen Yang fails to rouse, the clear Qi cannot ascend, and turbid Yin obstructs the channels of the ear, producing ear disease.

At the same time, since the Spleen governs transformation and transportation, in people with Spleen-Stomach weakness the body's fluids are poorly transformed and generate Phlegm; Chinese medicine holds that 'Phlegm-Fire' also causes tinnitus — with generalized heaviness, lightheadedness, chest oppression, and cough with copious phlegm, obstructing the Qi and Blood of the ear.

Spleen-Stomach weakness can be called the pattern most frequently differentiated by Chinese medicine over the past two thousand years, and the great majority of diseases also stem from it.

Tinnitus caused by poor circulation of blood and fluids in the body is also common. For example, there was a designer who went completely deaf in the right ear simply from napping face-down on his desk; the physician's diagnosis was that his habit of substituting coffee for water had, over time, thickened his blood, blocking the blood vessels beside the ear and causing a 'stroke of the ear.'

From the meridian perspective, the channels passing through the ear are not limited to the Triple Burner channel: taking the Gallbladder, Triple Burner, Small Intestine, Large Intestine, and Stomach channels as examples, all are related to the Spleen-Stomach digestive system — so the appearance of tinnitus in Spleen-Stomach weakness is no surprise either!

4. Qi stagnation with Blood stasis, and obesity

Whichever meridian pattern underlies the tinnitus is actually not the crux, because chronic tinnitus is generally produced by long-term blockage of Qi and Blood in certain meridians; so simply unblocking the relevant meridians, muscle adhesions, vascular blockages, and so on can relieve the tinnitus.

Simply put, when a person exhibits a particular 'meridian pattern' long-term and it becomes a 'meridian constitution,' it means certain meridians in the body have long been blocked and obstructed; after long accumulation, whole-body Qi stagnation with Blood stasis develops, and a certain proportion of people will develop refractory tinnitus.

Because this kind of meridian blockage must accumulate over a period of at least several years, even several decades, this chronic tinnitus usually appears in the middle-aged and elderly and is less likely to appear in the young.

After long-term blockage of Qi, Blood, and meridians, channel-sinew pathology inevitably appears; the currently popular myofascial trigger-point therapy can be applied to locate the adhered muscles, and kneading them open brings improvement. At the same time one should check whether the cervical spine has already degenerated and is compressing nerves to cause the tinnitus.

The muscles and cervical vertebrae of the head, face, neck, and back all affect the ear.

Lai Ren-Tsung, president of the Taiwan Tinnitus Society, has proposed that obesity is also a major cause of tinnitus. He shared the case of a Chinese physician in mainland China who specializes in treating tinnitus, whose secrets of treatment were 'a vegetarian diet' and 'going to bed before 10 p.m.': avoiding animal fats and getting sufficient sleep naturally lowers the likelihood of weight gain, allowing successful weight control and improvement of the tinnitus.

Most of the time, ear problems can be improved, even cured, through meridian or physical therapies (acupuncture and acupoint massage, tuina of the relevant muscles, spinal adjustment, and so on), improved lifestyle habits, or release of stress — with the correct method it is not difficult at all.

Summarized in a single sentence: if a person cultivates health long-term, keeps the meridians of the whole body unobstructed, and continually keeps the mind relaxed, it is almost impossible for tinnitus to appear; and even if it does appear, it can be cured very quickly.

So-called 'tinnitus' refers to perceiving noise (ringing, light tapping, cicada-like chirping, low roaring, and so on) when the external environment is producing no sound. Because tinnitus patients frequently present hearing deficits, 'tinnitus' and 'deafness' are often discussed together.

According to statistics, more than 45 million people in the United States are troubled by tinnitus, and roughly 15% of all humanity is affected by it. As time passes, tinnitus often becomes progressively worse.

Some tinnitus sufferers consequently become low in mood, anxious, or unable to concentrate. In 10% of people the tinnitus is caused by diabetes, and 1% are troubled by chronic tinnitus for their entire lives — which sounds like a rather terrifying prospect.

Tinnitus is not a disease in itself but a symptom with many causes. The causes of tinnitus are very numerous, for example: trauma, earwax impaction, tympanic membrane perforation, noise-induced injury, and so on can all produce tinnitus.

Certain diseases can present with tinnitus, for example: diabetes, facial nerve palsy, herpes zoster viral infection, cardiovascular disease, Meniere's disease, sinusitis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, depression, otitis media, stroke, and brain tumors such as acoustic neuroma, among others.

Some people hear the sound of their own blood vessels, or have tinnitus with a blocked-ear sensation produced by adhesions of the muscles near the ear — the causes are simply too complex.

Nevertheless, a certain proportion of people are diagnosed with no other disease yet present simple tinnitus, and the cause remains unknown despite every kind of examination. At this point the mysterious meridians of Chinese medicine can be applied to explain it, providing a different line of thinking.

Dry, rough eyes are a symptom the ancients already had a thousand years ago. Antiquity had no such term as 'dry eye syndrome,' but it did have the term 'dry and rough eyes' (mu gan se). The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic records it under the name 'despoliation of Essence' (duo jing); the Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun states 'when the humors are exhausted, the eyes are rough'; the Zheng Zhi Zhun Sheng mentions 'dryness, roughness, and blurred vision,' and so on.

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that the main cause of dry eyes is 'Yin depletion and Blood Deficiency,' for the Inner Classic speaks of the 'damage of the five taxations,' and the first of these is 'prolonged use of the eyes damages the Blood.'

So when a person's body is Blood Deficient, dry eyes readily appear. Chinese medicine further speaks of concepts such as 'the Liver stores the Blood,' 'the Liver opens into the eyes,' 'the Spleen manages the Blood,' 'the Heart governs the Blood,' and so on; dry eyes are therefore closely related to the Heart, Spleen, and Liver of Chinese medicine.

The tears of the eyes also belong to the fluids (jin-ye) spoken of in Chinese medicine; when a person's body is 'Dry-Hot,' insufficiency of fluids appears, and hence the eyes become dry and itchy.

All of the content above will have been seen by anyone with even a slight interest in Chinese medicine — utterly uniform, cliched, abstract, and offering nothing new, read without being understood. Is it not so?

If the causes of dry eyes could be detected with instruments and understood through data-driven analysis, more modern people would be convinced — and meridian testing can achieve exactly this purpose.

The analysis above belongs to 'zang-fu pattern differentiation,' while meridian testing belongs to 'meridian pattern differentiation.' To analyze diseases of the eye, one must first ask: which meridians lead to the eyes? According to the meridian authority Lin Yun-Gui's Illustrated Guide to the Meridians, fully 15 channels lead to the eyes (Note 1).

Summarizing these meridians, the principal ones are the Liver, Heart, Gallbladder, Stomach, Small Intestine, Triple Burner, and Bladder channels. How exactly do these abstract meridians affect the eyes and produce dryness?

From long-term observation of some Cloud TCM members, it emerges that the meridian phenomena shaping dry eyes can be divided into the following 3 steps:

Step 1: Fatigue shapes Liver channel Excess and Gallbladder channel abnormality

In anyone who regularly stays up late, is under heavy stress, and accumulates fatigue — regardless of whether the eyes are heavily used — the Liver channel in the body has a very high probability of beginning to show Excess. In most people the Gallbladder channel is long-term Deficient; in habitual night-owls, the Gallbladder channel converts to Excess.

After staying up late and excessive fatigue, the Liver and Gallbladder channels begin to become abnormal.

Dry, gritty eyes are a symptom common among modern people and are often discussed together with 'dry eye syndrome.' However, ocular dryness may be only a transient phenomenon; when a person has dry eyes long-term it may indeed be dry eye syndrome, but the appearance of dry eyes does not necessarily mean dry eye syndrome.

When a person's eyes are dry, there are often concurrent symptoms such as eye redness, burning, dry itching, foreign-body sensation, heavy eyelids, photophobia, and so on. According to data from the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), among people over 50, about 3.2 million women and 1.68 million men have dry eye syndrome, and roughly 26 million Americans experience dry eyes.

There are many causes of dry eyes, the chief one being overuse of the eyes. Modern people make heavy use of computers and digital devices, staring at the screen in front of them for 7-8 hours at a stretch; excessive concentration unconsciously reduces the number of blinks, so the eyes cannot be supplied with enough tear moisture and become dry.

Modern people often work overtime rushing projects and stay up late at the computer, remain long-term in environments with too little humidity (for example: air-conditioned rooms), which accelerates the evaporation of tears in a drying environment, or wear contact lenses — all of which make the eyes dry.

Age is a major factor in dry eyes: in anyone over 50, the state of ocular dryness grows progressively worse. Certain diseases such as thyroid disease, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjogren's syndrome may also lead to reduced tear secretion.

Most of the time, dry eyes improve simply by blinking to produce tears, or after instilling clean normal saline. Applying warm compresses to the eyes, using a humidifier to correct indoor dryness, drinking more water to replenish fluids, resting more, and using an air purifier to reduce airborne dust or pollution can all bring improvement.

Severe dry eye syndrome is discussed in another article. For those whose eye use is not heavy yet whose ocular dryness has no identifiable cause, this is exactly where Chinese medical theory is best suited to provide an explanation and a new line of thinking.

A foreign-body sensation in the throat is an old complaint that has troubled the Chinese for more than a thousand years. Records of this symptom exist from early antiquity.

The Jin Gui Yao Lue (Essentials from the Golden Cabinet) describes it as 'a feeling in the throat as if a piece of roasted meat were lodged there'; the Gu Jin Yi Jian (Medical Mirror Ancient and Modern) calls it 'plum-pit Qi' (mei he qi), vividly depicting that foreign-body sensation which 'can neither be coughed out nor swallowed down.'

Traditional Chinese medicine assigns 'foreign-body sensation in the throat' to the category of 'constraint patterns' (yu zheng), mostly caused by emotional discontent and obstruction of the Qi dynamic.

The ancients held that emotions are the main cause of the foreign-body sensation in the throat.

That is to say, the ancients had long since attributed this symptom to emotional factors. The most common pattern is 'Liver Qi stagnation with Phlegm and Qi mutually binding.'

The typical presentation is: a pronounced foreign-body sensation, aggravated during emotional fluctuations, accompanied by chest oppression and hypochondriac distension, frequent sighing, and depression with irritability; the tongue is pale red with a thin white or white greasy coating, and the pulse is mostly wiry and slippery.

According to the description in the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, a branch of the Liver channel passes through the diaphragm and pours into the Lung, while its main course ascends along the back of the throat to the nasopharynx, then connects with the eyes and reaches up to the vertex.

This channel distribution means that when Liver Qi is disordered, it easily affects the throat and produces the foreign-body sensation (plum-pit Qi).

When the Liver's free-coursing function is impeded and the movement of the Qi dynamic is not smooth, the early stage commonly manifests as chest oppression, rib-side pain, and a tendency to sigh.

If the Qi stagnation persists for 3 to 6 months, throat discomfort may appear. If the Qi stagnation lasts a year or more, it readily develops further into the state of 'Phlegm and Qi mutually binding' — formless Phlegm produced by disordered fluid metabolism.

Going further, this 'Phlegm-Qi mutual binding' is often accompanied by 'Spleen Deficiency with Phlegm-Damp.' Patients not only have a sensation of sticky phlegm in the throat but also commonly show fatigue and lack of strength, poor appetite, and loose, soft stools; the tongue is pale and swollen with tooth marks and a white greasy coating, and the pulse is soggy and slippery.

This is caused by Spleen Deficiency generating Dampness, the Dampness gathering into Phlegm, and the Phlegm further obstructing the airway.

All of the above is only theory — what is it like in practice? From the several hundred meridian patterns of 'foreign-body sensation in the throat' at Cloud TCM, it emerges that over 60% belong to the 'composite meridian pattern' and the 'Iron Triangle meridian pattern.'

Among them, the 'Iron Triangle pattern transformed into extreme Fire-Heat' reaches as high as 45% or more — this is the classic meridian pattern associated with emotional stress and depressed mood, fully corroborating ancient Chinese medical theory.

The two meridian patterns in which plum-pit Qi most commonly appears.

Since these meridian patterns may persist for decades or more, a certain proportion of people develop 'Phlegm-Qi mutual binding' and naturally experience the foreign-body sensation in the throat.

The method of improvement is likewise simple: use Chinese herbs to course the Liver and rectify Qi, fortify the Spleen and transform Phlegm, and rectify Qi and harmonize the middle, and rapid improvement follows; the most commonly used formula is Ban Xia Hou Po Tang (Pinellia and Magnolia Bark Decoction).

In daily life one can frequently massage Taichong (LR-3), Neiguan (PC-6), and Danzhong (CV-17), which course the Liver and rectify Qi. Combine these with Zusanli (ST-36), Fenglong (ST-40), and Yinlingquan (SP-9) to transform Phlegm and dissipate binding, and Sanyinjiao (SP-6) and Zhaohai (KI-6) to enrich Yin and direct Fire downward, and recovery can be accelerated.

In addition, traditional Chinese medicine also holds that Yin Deficiency with effulgent Fire can cause a foreign-body sensation in the throat, because the Kidney channel also passes through the throat: when Deficiency Fire flames upward, the throat is dry, rough, and burning, and the foreign-body sensation is accompanied by dry mouth, vexation and insomnia, and heat in the palms and soles, with a red tongue with scant coating and a thin, rapid pulse.

Since the Lung and Heart channels also pass through the throat, when there is constrained Heat of the Heart and Liver or Fire-Heat of the Lung, and constrained Qi transforms into Fire, there appears burning pain of the throat with a pronounced foreign-body sensation, impatience and irritability, bitter taste and dry mouth, and insomnia with profuse dreaming; the tongue is red with a yellow coating and the pulse wiry and rapid.

In fact, in the 'Iron Triangle pattern transformed into extreme Fire-Heat,' the Kidney channel is generally Deficient, but in some people it converts to Excess — this is a phenomenon of Yin Deficiency with effulgent Fire.

Fire-Hot Excess of the Lung, Triple Burner, and Large Intestine channels causes the entire chest to become Fire-Hot, producing Heart Fire and Lung Fire, and hence the throat feels very uncomfortable.

Chinese medicine holds that a foreign-body sensation in the throat is usually related to the emotions, and treatment must regulate body and mind together — one cannot rely on medication alone.

In daily life one must keep the emotions relaxed and flowing, avoiding suppression or anxiety; deep breathing and meditation can be practiced. The diet should avoid spicy, fried, and chilled items and overly sweet foods; those with Phlegm-Damp should eat less rich, fatty, sweet, and heavy food — only then can prevention and treatment reach the root.

As far back as the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic there are mentions of 'kou mi' (oral erosion), 'kou chuang' (mouth sores), and 'kou yang' (oral ulceration) — the similar terms are very numerous.

Clinically, 'sores in the mouth' and 'sores at the corners of the mouth' are discussed separately, but since their formative causes are similar, they are discussed together here.

The 'Mouth and Tongue' chapter of the Jing Yue Quan Shu (Complete Works of Jing-Yue) points out that sores of the mouth and tongue appear on the surface to be caused by excessive Heat in the Upper Burner and can be treated by taking cold-cool Chinese herbs.

Many people wake in the morning to find unexplained oral ulcers, and most people in Asia will instinctively assume: 'Excessive internal Fire!'

Mouth sores, also called 'aphthous stomatitis,' are ulcers of the soft tissue inside the mouth — that is, oral ulcers — commonly appearing on the tongue, the soft palate, the inner side of the lips, and the inner side of both cheeks. The inflamed site shows a raised lesion with a white round center and a red rim, or a wound that is slow to heal; this is what people commonly call a 'broken mouth.'

A similar phenomenon occurring at the mouth is 'angular cheilitis,' commonly known as 'sore mouth corners' — acute or chronic inflammation at the junction of the upper and lower lips. The most obvious symptoms are blisters, redness, erosion, crusting, desquamation, or ulceration on one or both sides of the lips.

As for the causes of mouth ulcers and angular cheilitis, modern medicine has found the etiology to be extremely varied. Urticaria (hives) is a very common skin disease and can be considered a form of skin allergy. It is characterized by raised red or pale wheals on the skin, accompanied by an intense itching sensation.

Acute urticaria usually subsides and heals naturally, but it may appear repeatedly at different sites. Most of the time the cause of onset is unknown, and modern medicine commonly classifies it as an allergic phenomenon.

For example: it may appear after viral infection, insect bites, temperature changes (too cold or too hot), wind exposure, sun exposure, emotional stress, pollen, irritation from plants such as nettles, or after eating seafood (fish, shrimp, crab).

It may also be caused by injections of serum, penicillin, and other drugs, or by irritation from dust, hair and dander, molds, and the like. Chronic idiopathic urticaria is mostly caused by abnormalities of the immune system.

Modern medicine commonly treats acute urticaria with 'antihistamines' or 'corticosteroids.' Severe or refractory chronic urticaria may even require immunosuppressants or biologic agents.

For such a strange disease, one may also consider understanding it from the perspective of Chinese medicine — in particular, certain 'meridian constitutions' are more prone to developing urticaria.

Because the members reporting themselves troubled by neurasthenia over the past several years have been truly numerous, by summarizing these meridian patterns one can identify several principal underlying causes, chiefly the following:

1. Liver Qi stagnation, Heart-Spleen dual Deficiency, Heart Blood Deficiency

Traditional Chinese medicine holds that 'the Heart governs the blood and vessels.' When a person worries and deliberates excessively, Heart Blood is consumed and damaged, leading to insufficiency of Heart Blood, with symptoms such as palpitations, insomnia, profuse dreaming, easy fright, forgetfulness, dizziness, and so on.

When the Heart's mental-spiritual functions are disordered, this may manifest as disquiet of the Heart-spirit, mental abstraction, sorrow and a desire to weep, inability to control one's emotions, vexation and turmoil in the heart, restless sleep, and repeated yawning; in severe cases even abnormalities of speech may appear.

The ancients called this symptom-complex 'visceral agitation' (zang zao); it bears some resemblance to what is now called neurasthenia, and it is improved with Gan Mai Da Zao Tang (Licorice, Wheat and Jujube Decoction).

The ancients held that 'worry damages the Spleen': excessive thinking not only damages the Heart's Blood but also affects the functions of the Spleen and Stomach — the vital parts of the body that generate Qi and Blood; when both are impaired, the spirit cannot be kept stable.

The ancients held that 'worry damages the Spleen' — excessive thinking harms the Spleen and Stomach.

Chinese medicine also holds that 'the Liver governs the Qi of the whole body,' directing the movement of all Qi within the human body. Liver Qi must stretch out and flow freely; if it becomes 'constrained and stagnant,' the seven emotions (joy, anger, worry, thought, sorrow, fear, fright) cannot be regulated smoothly — so Liver Qi stagnation also produces neurasthenia.

If this Liver Qi stagnation accumulates in the body for a period of time, the phenomenon of 'transformation into Fire' appears, and at that point the neurasthenia becomes still more severe.

The extreme manifestation of the Iron Triangle meridian pattern.

Under normal circumstances, Water and Fire blend together, and Heart and Kidney should cooperate with each other. When the two cannot commune smoothly, the state of Heart-Kidney non-interaction results.

The human brain is a very mysterious organ — and in fact it is remarkably hard-wearing! The nerve cells of the cerebral cortex are like tumbler dolls that can work overtime continuously: as long as they are given sufficient sleep and rest, they can rapidly recover their vigor and throw themselves into the fray once more.

However, under the enormous pressures of modern society, neurasthenia has become the hidden enemy of many people. When the cranial nerves are overused for long periods — like a marathon run without pause — there comes a moment when the limit of tolerance is exceeded.

Modern people suffer information anxiety and generally overuse their brains.

When a person is struck by neurasthenia, his life is as if placed under a strange spell. Forgetting things becomes commonplace, like being a goldfish with only fleeting memory.

He is listless all day, as though all the vitality of life had been drained away. Whatever he does, he cannot summon any energy, and in the end he only wants to find a quiet corner to sit or lie down.

His reactions slow, and he grows indifferent to the people and things around him, which may lead others to mistake it for depression. His emotional swings are large: over some small matter he may sink into deep gloom, or suddenly erupt in anger.

Sleep is no longer an easy matter: he is often startled awake by the slightest sound, and then tosses and turns, unable to fall asleep again.

This state is often classified as 'psychoneurosis,' 'autonomic nervous system dysregulation,' or 'psychosomatic disorder.' But on examination at the hospital, one often receives an answer that leaves one not knowing whether to laugh or cry: 'There is nothing wrong with you!' — which makes one feel all the more helpless.

At this point, Chinese medicine provides another angle from which to view and treat neurasthenia, offering an entirely new line of thinking!
